<term>Ceremony</term>: The formal religious protocol observed during the administration of the sacraments.

<term>Worship Service</term>: <note>original: "culte"</note> The communal gathering for prayer, singing, and scripture reading, centered around the sermon.

Plate 12.

->No. 1.<-

## Meeting of those who in Amsterdam are called **Collegiants**.

These do not form a separate church or congregation, but only private societies or gatherings of religious, learned people from all Christian denominations. In these meetings, each person freely explains his thoughts or opinions regarding one or another doctrine of <term>Religion<note>The original Dutch uses "Godsdienst," which literally means "service to God."</note></term>, or a passage in the Holy Scripture. They are united solely by their love for liberty of conscience in religion.

---

->No. 2.<-

## Their **Communion celebration** at **Rijnsburg**, a village near **Leiden**.

This is where they primarily hold their assembly and where, notwithstanding the differences in their ideas, they unite and partake of the <term>Lord’s Supper<note>The "Avondmaals-viering" refers to the ritual of Communion or the Eucharist, which the Collegiants practiced in a simplified, egalitarian manner.</note></term> together as brothers. They do so while lamenting the misery of Christendom, which, being divided by so many conflicting opinions, finds itself exposed to the mockery of <term>freethinkers<note>In the 18th century, "vrijgeesten" or freethinkers were seen as those who rejected traditional religious authority in favor of reason, often viewed with suspicion by the orthodox.</note></term> and unbelievers.

<term>Collegiants</term>, <term>Amsterdam</term>, <term>Rijnsburg</term>, <term>Leiden</term>, <term>Communion celebration</term>, <term>Religion</term>, <term>Holy Scripture</term>, <term>liberty of conscience</term>, <term>freethinkers</term>

<summary>This page describes the Collegiants, a 17th and 18th-century Dutch religious group that valued open theological discussion and liberty of conscience over formal church structures. <header>Plate 13.</header>

# The Baptism of the <term>Rhijnsburgers</term> <note>The Rhijnsburgers, or Collegiants, were a 17th-century Dutch religious group that emerged from the Remonstrant tradition. They met in "colleges" and were known for their practice of adult baptism by total immersion in the town of Rhijnsburg.</note>.

This is a ceremony in which the person who desires to be baptized—after having made their <term>confession of faith</term> <note>original: "belijdenis des geloofs"</note> before the entire assembly—descends into a type of fountain or pond located behind the Rhijnsburgers' meeting house, accompanied by the person who is to perform the baptism, in order to be <term>immersed</term> <note>original: "gedompeld"</note> in the water. 

If the person is a man, he is dressed in a white shirt and trousers; if it is a woman, she wears a shift and an outer garment, to the bottom of which several pieces of lead are attached <note>These weights were a practical measure to ensure that the woman’s skirts did not float to the surface during immersion, thereby preserving her modesty.</note>. Afterward, they are solemnly exhorted within the assembly to remain steadfast in the observance of the <term>Divine commandments</term> <note>original: "Goddelijke geboden"</note>.

<summary>A description of the adult immersion baptism practiced by the Rhijnsburgers (Collegiants), including details on the location, the confession of faith, and the specific attire worn for modesty.</summary>
<keywords>Rhijnsburgers, Collegiants, adult baptism, immersion, confession of faith, religious rituals, modesty weights, Rhijnsburg</keywords>

<header>Plate 13 (Illustration)</header>

# The Meeting House of the <term>Rhijnsburgers</term> <note>This building, known as "Het Grote Huis" (The Great House) in Rhijnsburg, served as the central meeting place for the Collegiants. The baptismal pond mentioned previously was located in the gardens behind this structure.</note>

->[An engraving of a social gathering before a large brick residence]<-

This fine engraving depicts a substantial two-story brick residence, typical of 18th-century Dutch architecture. The house is constructed with a steep, tiled roof featuring dormer windows and two slender, spire-like chimneys. The facade is characterized by many windows with functional shutters and several doorways where figures can be seen entering the building or peering out at the crowd. To the left, a portion of an adjacent wing or a neighboring building is visible, suggesting the scale of the complex.

A large assembly of men and women, dressed in the formal attire of the mid-1700s, occupies the courtyard and the street in front of the house. The men are generally dressed in <term>justacorps</term> <note>A long, knee-length coat that was a staple of men's fashion in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note>, breeches, and various styles of hats, including the popular <term>tricorne</term> <note>A three-cornered hat with the brim turned up.</note>. The women wear voluminous dresses with petticoats and are adorned with white caps or bonnets. The figures are arranged in several conversational clusters, creating a sense of a significant social and religious occasion.

The background shows a dense line of trees rising behind the house, while the sky is filled with light, delicately etched clouds. A noticeable vertical seam on the left side of the print indicates that this was originally a <term>fold-out plate</term> <note>original: "hors-texte"</note>, a large illustration folded into the binding of the book to provide a panoramic view of the scene.

<summary>A visual representation of the Collegiant meeting house in Rhijnsburg, showing a large crowd of 18th-century worshippers gathered outside the "Great House."</summary>

Plate 13.

# The Baptism of the Rijnsburgers

A ceremony in which the person who desires to be baptized—after having made their <term>confession of faith</term> <note>original: "belijdenis des geloofs"; a public declaration of one's religious convictions and commitment to the community's values.</note> before the entire congregation—descends with the person who is to perform the baptism into a type of fountain or pond located behind the meeting place of the <term>Rijnsburgers</term> <note>Also known as Collegiants, this was a Dutch religious group founded in the 17th century that rejected formal church hierarchy and practiced adult baptism by full immersion in the town of Rijnsburg.</note>, in order to be immersed in the water. If it is a man, he is dressed in a white shirt and trousers; if it is a woman, she wears a shift and an outer garment, to the bottom of which several pieces of lead are attached <note>These lead weights were a practical addition to ensure the woman’s clothing remained submerged for the sake of modesty during the full immersion.</note>. Following this, they are earnestly exhorted within the assembly to remain steadfast in the observance of the Divine commandments.

<term>The Baptism</term>, <term>Rijnsburgers</term>, <term>confession of faith</term>, <term>fountain</term>, <term>pond</term>, <term>immersed</term>, <term>Divine commandments</term>

<summary>This text describes the ritual of adult immersion baptism practiced by the Rijnsburgers, highlighting the specific attire used and the communal exhortation that followed the ceremony.</summary>

# Plate 2.

**A. 1. 2. Communion bread** of the Greeks. These are unleavened <note>While the text says 'unleavened' (ongerezen), most Eastern Orthodox traditions actually use leavened bread called Prosphora; the author may be mistaken or describing a specific variant.</note> breads, which the Greeks and Muscovites <note>A historical term for Russians</note> use in their Mass; they are marked with a single or a double cross. The letters found on the four corners mean: *Jesus Christ Conquers* <note>original Greek: Ιησῦς χρισός Νικᾶ</note>, that is: **JESUS C<gloss>H</gloss>RISTUS** is the victor.

**B. The Star** [as they call it] which they place over the dish with the consecrated bread so that the linen cloth, with which it is covered, does not touch the bread.

**C. The Bishop**, holding in both his hands—marked g. and h.—the candlesticks of two and three branches <note>These are the 'dikirion' and 'trikirion' used by a bishop to bless the faithful.</note>.

**D. The Fan** <note>A liturgical fan or 'ripidion,' often depicting a multi-winged seraph, used to keep insects away from the Eucharist and to symbolize the presence of angels.</note>.

**E. 1. 2. The Qurban** <term>Qurban: A word of Semitic origin meaning an offering or sacrifice to God</term>, or communion bread of the Copts <note>Egyptian Christians</note>, upon which various crosses can be seen in raised relief, all arranged in order with the inscription: *The Holy* and *the Strong* <note>original Greek: Ἄγιος Ἴχυρος (Agios Ischyros)</note>.

The priest (labeled C) appears here, dressed in all his vestments, such as:
**a. The long robe**.
**b. The Stole** or cross-band.
**c. The sleeves** of the robe.
**d. The round cloak**, which hangs from the front down to the belt and from the back down to the calf of the leg.
**e. A type of collar or neckband**.
**f. A square piece of cloth**, which hangs from the belt <note>This is likely the 'epigonation,' a symbolic thigh-shield representing the 'sword of the Spirit.'</note>.

## Mourning of the Greek women at Ramah.

Or hired professional mourners <note>original: "omgekogte klaagvrouwen"</note>, who, after having sat around the grave for half an hour, rise to form a circle and struggle together <note>The Dutch "worstelen" suggests a rhythmic, physical movement or a swaying ritual common in traditional mourning</note> while raising a terrible cry.

---

->No. 2.<-

## Solemn baptism of the Greek and Syrian Christians in the Jordan River.

Whereby everyone, without distinction of gender <term>gender: translated from the archaic Dutch "kunne"</term>, entirely naked and mixed together, throws themselves with the greatest piety into the Jordan to baptize themselves and one another; some take moistened cloths with them, while others scoop water into bottles, and still others even take some of the earth and the herbs that grow on the banks of the river back to their own country. <note>It was common for pilgrims to bring home "souvenirs" of soil or water from the Holy Land as contact relics.</note>

Plate 7.

## Memorial Service for the Deceased among the Armenians.

This practice is especially in use among the *Armenians of Julpha* <note>New Julfa, the Armenian quarter of Isfahan, Iran, known for its distinct cultural and religious traditions</note>; they celebrate it on August 26, [being the feast of the holy cross <note>original: "heilige kruis"</note>,] with burning wax candles and ignited fires into which they throw incense, all accompanied by shouting and wailing. This mournful ceremony is performed solely by women dressed in white, with the exception of some priests dressed in black, who are compensated for their service.

## Memorial celebration for the deceased among the Armenians,

Which is especially in use among the Armenians of *Julpha* <note>New Julfa, the Armenian quarter of Isfahan, established in 1606 by Shah Abbas I</note>; they celebrate this on the 26th of August, [being the feast of the <term>Holy Cross|an important religious observance in the Armenian Apostolic Church, traditionally involving the blessing of the four corners of the world</term>,] with burning wax candles and lit fires into which they throw incense, all accompanied by shouting and wailing. This mournful ceremony is performed solely by women dressed in white, except for some priests dressed in black, who are compensated for their service.

PLATE VII.

->*The COMMEMORATION of the DEAD among the ARMENIANS.*<-

<image-desc>A detailed nocturnal engraving depicting a scene in an Armenian cemetery. Numerous figures, dressed in long robes and veils, are gathered among flat grave markers. Several small fires burn throughout the graveyard, casting light on the mourners and sending plumes of smoke into the air. Candles are placed on several of the tombstones. In the foreground, people are shown in various postures of grief and devotion: some sit together in small groups, others stand, and one figure is prostrate on the ground. To the right, a stone structure with a prominent pointed arch houses another group of people. In the background, rugged mountains are silhouetted against a night sky dotted with stars.</image-desc>

This memorial celebration for the deceased is a significant ritual, particularly among the Armenians residing in *Julpha* <note>New Julfa, the Armenian quarter of Isfahan, established in 1606 by Shah Abbas I after the forced resettlement of Armenians from the Caucasus</note>. They observe this ceremony on the 26th of August, which corresponds with the feast of the <term>Holy Cross|The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, one of the five major "Tabernacle" feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church</term>. 

The ritual is conducted at night, characterized by the lighting of wax candles and large fires upon the graves. Mourners cast incense into these flames, creating the dense smoke seen in the engraving, while the air is filled with ritual shouting and wailing. This mournful ceremony is performed almost exclusively by women, who are traditionally dressed in white mourning garments <note>While black is common today, white was historically used for mourning in various Eastern Christian and Persian-influenced cultures</note>. They are accompanied by priests dressed in black vestments, who are compensated for leading the prayers and services.

<vocab>Commemoration, Armenians, the dead, cemetery, funeral rite, engraving, night</vocab>

<summary>This plate illustrates the nocturnal memorial rituals of the Armenian community in New Julfa, Isfahan, featuring the use of fire, incense, and white mourning dress during the feast of the Holy Cross.</summary>
<keywords>Armenians, New Julfa, Isfahan, mourning rituals, Holy Cross, funeral customs, Persian Armenians, 17th-century traditions</keywords>

## The baptism of the Russians,

Which occurs with much ceremony, such as the immersion of the child in a deep vessel filled with water, giving a grain of salt into the mouth, anointing it after <gloss>the</gloss> baptism, and putting a clean shirt on it, etc. <note>This "clean shirt" refers to the *kryzhma*, a white garment symbolizing the soul's purity after the rite.</note>

## The burial of the Russians,

Which is of little consequence among the poor and the lower classes, but magnificent among persons of rank, owing to the numerous following and the large number of hired professional mourners. <note>In many Eastern European cultures, professional mourners were women hired to wail and sing traditional laments.</note> One also gives to the deceased a safe-conduct letter, or rather a letter of absolution <note>original: "schuldvergiftenis"</note> in their coffin, and even today one sometimes hires a priest to pray for the deceased in a hut near the grave during the mourning period, which lasts forty <gloss>days</gloss>.
</insert>

# PLATE IX.

<meta>No. 1</meta>

->THE RUSSIAN BAPTISM<-

<insert>
No. 1

## The baptism of the Russians

This ceremony is performed with great solemnity and specific rituals. These include the full immersion of the infant into a deep vessel filled with water, placing a grain of salt in the child's mouth, and anointing the body following <gloss>the</gloss> baptism. Finally, the child is dressed in a clean shirt to complete the rite. <note>The "clean shirt" refers to the *kryzhma*, a white garment symbolizing the soul's purity and new life after the sacrament.</note>
</insert>

---

<meta>No. 2</meta>

->THE RUSSIAN FUNERALS<-

<insert>
No. 2

## The burial of the Russians

Funeral rites are quite simple among the poor and lower classes, but they become magnificent displays among people of high rank. These elaborate ceremonies are characterized by a massive funeral procession and the presence of many hired professional mourners. <note>In many Eastern European cultures, professional mourners were women hired to wail and sing traditional laments to honor the deceased.</note> A "safe-conduct" letter—or more accurately, a letter of absolution <note>original: "schuldvergiftenis" - a Dutch term for the forgiveness of sins</note>—is placed in the coffin with the deceased. Even today, it is sometimes the custom to hire a priest to pray for the departed in a small hut near the grave throughout the mourning period, which lasts for forty <gloss>days</gloss>. <note>The forty-day period is significant in Orthodox tradition, representing the time the soul travels before its final placement.</note>
</insert>

<note>During a **Conclave**, cardinals were locked within the Vatican palace. Because there were not enough permanent rooms, small temporary wooden apartments, or "cells," were constructed for them in the large halls and chapels.</note>

# Plates 4 and 5, belonging together.

<insert>
The Pope solemnly takes possession of the High Priesthood in the Church of St. John Lateran, which is the principal church of all those existing within the Christian jurisdiction of the Pope.
</insert>

The manner in which the Pope solemnly takes possession of the High Priesthood <term>Opperpriesterschap: The office of the Supreme Pontiff</term> and the supreme authority over the Christian Church, in the Church of St. John Lateran, just as Clement XI <note>Pope Clement XI, who reigned from 1700 to 1721</note> did among others. In the first part, there appear the Musicians, the vanguard, all sorts of Pages, pack animals, etc. In the second part, the Roman Noblemen, the Papal officials, the Commissioners, the Governor of Rome, the Nephews and blood relatives of the Pope <note>Refers to the "Papal Nephews," a historical term for relatives of the Pope who held high office</note>, the Ambassadors of crowned heads, the Apostolic sub-deacon carrying the holy cross, etc. Then, the Pope seated in a litter <note>original: "draagkoets," referring here to a ceremonial sedan chair or carriage</note> or on a pack horse, amidst fifty Roman Noblemen, and led by a detachment of Cavalry under the command of a captain of the Swiss. Near His Holiness's litter was the Lord Chamberlain, then the Chief Cupbearer, the Private Secretaries, the Personal Physician, followed by the Swiss Guard. After these followed the Cardinals two by two, the Pope's bodyguard, the High Priests (*), the Archbishops, the Bishops, the Apostolic Chief Protonotary <note>original: "Oppergeregtsschrijver," a high-ranking legal official of the Papal court</note>, the members of the Court, and the Treasurers. Finally, the led horses, the trumpeters, and two companies of light Cavalry armed with lances.

This entire procession passed before the City Hall under a triumphal arch erected by the Roman people, and under another on the cattle market <note>The Campo Vaccino, which was the name for the Roman Forum at the time</note>, erected by the Duke of Parma.

The Clergy in <gloss>the</gloss> church of St. John Lateran come in a procession (+) to meet the parade, and there the Pope, seated upon a throne, receives the keys of the church as has been said before.

---

(*) The Patriarchs. (+) In Procession <note>original: "In Processie"</note>.

9 Jesus Christ accused before Pilate.
->*The PRIEST reads the <term>Epistle</term>.*<- <note>The Epistle is a reading from the New Testament letters. In this symbolic tradition, the movement to the side of the altar to read it represents Christ being brought before the Roman governor, Pilate.</note>

---

12 J.C. stripped to be scourged.
->*The PRIEST uncovers the <term>Chalice</term>.*<- <note>The Chalice is the cup used to hold the wine; uncovering it symbolizes Christ being stripped of his garments.</note>

---

15 Pilate washing his hands, declares J.C. innocent.
->*The PRIEST washes his hands.*<- <note>This ritual is known as the "Lavabo," where the priest asks for spiritual purity; here it mirrors Pilate's famous gesture of washing his hands to claim innocence of Christ's blood.</note>

<column-break/>

10 J.C., accused before Herod, answers nothing.
->*The Priest, bowing at the center of the ALTAR, says softly: <term>Cleanse my heart</term>, etc.*<- <note>original: "MUNDA COR." The full prayer is: "Cleanse my heart and my lips, O Almighty God..." Just as Jesus remained silent before Herod, the priest prays in a low, humble voice.</note>

---

13 J.C. bound to the Column and scourged.
->*The <term>Offering</term> of THE <term>Host</term>.*<- <note>The "Oblation" or offering of the bread (Host) represents Christ offering his body to be broken and beaten for humanity.</note>

---

16 J.C. covered with a Purple Robe.
->*The Priest, turned toward the People, says: <term>Pray, Brethren</term>.*<- <note>original: "ORATE FRATRES." This is an invitation to the congregation to join their prayers with his; symbolically, it recalls Christ being presented to the crowds in the purple robe of mockery.</note>

Plate 12.

->No. 1.<-

### Consecration of the Great Cross.

Whereby the Bishop, in the presence of the clergy, delivers a sermon and offers his prayer, after an altar server has lit three wax candles at the foot of the cross.

---

->No. 3.<-

### The Baptism of the Bell.

Which is performed through sprinkling, washing, rubbing, and anointing <note>Historical term for the solemn blessing of a church bell, so called because the rituals of washing and naming mirror those of a human baptism.</note>, while the Bishop and the clergy sing and offer prayers.

---

->No. 5.<-

### Censing the Bell.

By means of the censer <term>censer: a metal vessel (also called a thurible) in which incense is burned during religious ceremonies</term>, which is placed beneath the hanging bell.

<column-break/>

->No. 2.<-

### The Censing of the Cross.

Which is performed during the consecration, after three lit wax candles have been placed on the cross—specifically, one at the top and two on the arms of the same.

---

->No. 4.<-

### The Consecration of the Bell.

Which is performed in the name of the Holy Trinity, and involves giving it the name of a particular saint.

---

->No. 6.<-

### Consecration of a Statue.

Which is performed with sprinkling, the naming of the saint whom the statue represents, and—if it is an image of the Blessed Virgin—through a triple censing, hymns, prayers, signs of the cross, etc.

<vocab>Consecration, Bishop, sermon, prayer, wax candles, censing, cross, bell, sprinkling, anointing, censer, Trinity</vocab>

<summary>This page describes various Catholic liturgical consecrations, specifically the rituals for blessing large crosses, church bells (the "baptism of the bell"), and religious statues.</summary>
<keywords>liturgy, consecration, church bells, religious rituals, censing, iconography, Catholic tradition</keywords>

<note>The following sections correspond to the six panels depicted in the illustrations, detailing the ritual of <term>church consecration</term> (the formal dedication of a building for sacred use).</note>

**No. 1. The Writing of the Alphabets**
The Bishop uses his crozier to write the <term>Abecedarium</term>. By tracing both the Greek and Latin alphabets in the ashes, the Bishop symbolically takes possession of the space in the name of Christ, the Alpha and the Omega, representing the gathering of all nations into the Church.

**No. 2. The Diagram of the Ash-Cross**
A detailed view of the <term>ash-cross</term> (Dutch: *as-kruis*). The cross is drawn on the floor of the church using ashes or sand, stretching from one corner of the nave to the opposite corner.

**No. 3. The Consecration of the Altar**
The Bishop is shown at the altar, marking it with the sign of the cross using holy water. This act designates the altar as the "table of the Lord," the central point of the liturgy.

**No. 4. The Purification of the Church**
In this scene, the Bishop processes through the interior, sprinkling the floor and walls with holy water. This ritual cleanses the building of any secular or profane use, preparing it for its holy purpose.

**No. 5. The Translation of the Relics**
A solemn moment where the <term>relics</term> (sacred remains of saints) are carried into the church. Historically, a church was not considered fully consecrated until the relics were placed within the "sepulcher" or cavity of the altar.

**No. 6. The Conclusion of the Rite**
The final panel shows the clergy gathered at the end of the ceremony. After the anointings and the placement of relics, the church is now officially a sacred space, and the first Mass can be celebrated.

It explains the transition from a secular building to a consecrated house of worship through symbolic acts of writing, sprinkling, and the placement of relics.</summary>

# The Agnus Dei

**A. Accurate copy of the printed sheet of the**
**Agnus Dei**, which is a type of medal made in one side of [wax mixed with balsam], featuring a Lamb, with the inscription: **Agnus Dei qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis.** <note>The OCR text 'Agnus I miserer: nobis. VII' is a corrupted transcription of the Latin: 'Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.'</note> that is: *Lamb of God! who [takes away the sins of the world], have mercy on us*. as seen at letter **B**. The [other] side shows the image of one or another saint.
**C. The coat of arms of Pope Alexander VII**, who issued the first aforementioned sheet; the translation of the [blessing follows].
**D. The Scapulars**, being two pieces of certain woven [cloth] joined together, which most monastics wear to earn indulgences. <note>A scapular consists of two small squares of wool joined by strings, worn over the shoulders as a sign of devotion.</note> (\*) one piece [is worn on the chest, the other on the back].
**E. Rosary or Paternoster**, composed of five [decades]. <note>The term 'Paternoster' (Our Father) refers here to the string of prayer beads.</note>
**F. Ordinary Rosary decorated with Relics, and [crosses].**
**G. Ring**, which the Knights of Malta use to pray; the rose upon it turns by means of a spring, with a black point pointing to the fifteen numbers upon it, which represent the numbers or parts of the rosary mentioned above. <note>A mechanical 'rosary ring' used for counting prayers discreetly.</note>
**H. A portion or decade of the rosary.**
**I. Bread of St. Genevieve**, being a type of dry [biscuit or cake] which the followers of St. Genevieve distribute for the healing of [fevers]. <note>St. Genevieve is the patron saint of Paris; blessed bread was often distributed in her name for miraculous healing.</note>
**K. Consecrated copper medal** which the sisters of the rosary wear to preserve their chastity.

(\*) See *Halma, Dictionary, page 945, under the word: Scapulaire.*

# THE VIRTUES OF THE AGNVS DEI,
<note>Latin: "Lamb of God"</note>

Composed of Holy Chrism, Balsam, and pure wax. Extracted from the book called the *Ceremonial*, where, speaking of the Blessing of these items, the following words are found recorded at the end in this manner.

The thunders it chases;

### The Prayer that the Pope says at the Blessing of the Agnus Dei.

> That it may erase sins, that pardon may be obtained, and that it may confer graces.
> That upon touching and seeing it, Christians may be moved to praise God.
> That the crashing of the air, hail, snow, and tempests, the fury of the winds, and the thunders may be moderated and stopped.
> That before the Saving and glorious standard of the Cross, which is figured there, the evil spirits may be terrified and flee.
> That he who carries them may have power against the illusions, deceptions, craftiness, and frauds of the Devil and of evil spirits.
> That no tempest, adversity, pestilential or corrupt air, nor falling sickness <note>term: "mal caduc" — an old term for epilepsy</note>, no torment, sea storms, no fire, nor other injuries of the weather, may be able to offend, harm, or prejudice him who shall devoutly carry it upon himself.
> That in childbirth the Mother and the child may be preserved.
> That all those who carry it may always be in safety, that they may fear no peril, that they may have no fear of shadows, that no cruelty of the Devil may damage them, that they may not be deceived by men, that they may be exempt from all perils, from fire, from lightning, from torment, and tempests. And that women may give birth without labor, and be delivered from evil and from all danger.

->AT ROME, At the Printer of the Apostolic Chamber. 1662.<-
->with permission of the Superiors.<-

PLATE XVIII.

# THE VIRTUES OF THE AGNUS DEI,
<note>Latin: "Lamb of God"</note>

Composed of Holy Chrism <term>Holy Chrism: a consecrated oil used in baptism and other sacraments</term>, Balsam, and pure wax. Extracted from the book called the *Ceremonial*, where, speaking of their blessing, the following words are found recorded near the end in this manner:

->It is read that Pope Urban V sent three *Agnus Dei* to the Emperor of the Greeks, with these verses and words.<-

<columns>
It drives away thunder;
It erases sins;
It saves from fire,
And from drowning;
It guards against sudden death,
It puts Devils to flight,
And subdues enemies.
<column-break/>
Both the child and the Mother
Are placed out of danger;
For those who labor to make it;
It gives great power,
To those worthy to have it;
A part, however small,
Profits as much as the whole.
</columns>

### The Prayer that the Pope offers at the Blessing of the *Agnus Dei*.

>May it erase sins, may pardon be obtained, and may it confer graces. May Christians, upon touching and seeing it, be moved to praise God. May the noise of the air, hail, snow, and storms, the fury of the winds and thunder be moderated and halted. May the evil spirits be terrified and flee before the saving and glorious standard of the Cross, which is depicted upon it. May he who carries them have power against the illusions, deceptions, cunning, and frauds of the Devil and of evil spirits. May no storm, adversity, pestilential or corrupt air, nor falling sickness <term>falling sickness: an old term for epilepsy</term>, nor any torment, sea storms, any fire, or other injuries of the weather be able to offend, harm, or prejudice him who shall devoutly carry it upon himself. May the Mother and the child be preserved during childbirth. May all those who carry it be always in safety; may they fear no peril, may they have no fear of shadows, may no cruelty of the Devil harm them, may they not be deceived by men, and may they be exempt from all perils of fire, lightning, torment, and storms. And may women give birth without labor, and be delivered from evil and all danger.

->IN ROME, At the Printer of the Apostolic Chamber. 1662.<-
->with permission of the Superiors.<-

---

**A.** An exact copy of the printed sheet that the Pope gives with the *Agnus Dei*, which is a type of wax medal representing a Lamb, as seen at letter **B**. This medal has the image of some Saint on the reverse side.
**C.** The Coat of Arms of Pope Alexander VII, who provided the original of the aforementioned sheet **A**.
**D.** The Scapular <term>Scapular: two small pieces of cloth joined by string, worn over the shoulders as a sign of devotion</term>.
**E.** The Rosary, a prayer chain composed of 15 decades.
**F.** An ordinary rosary, enriched with a Reliquary, etc.
**G.** A ring which the Knights of Malta use to say their Rosary; the wheel on top turns and clicks, marking with a small black dot on the 10 numbers around it the number of decades already recited.
**H.** A decade <note>a single-decade rosary</note> for saying one's prayers.
**I.** Bread of Saint Genevieve (or a type of small dry biscuit), which the Monks of Saint Genevieve distribute for the relief of fever.
**K.** A Blessed copper medal that the Sisters of Charity in Paris wear on their rosary to preserve their virginity <note>or "purity of life"</note>.

Plate 18.

# The Agnus Dei.
<note>Latin: "Lamb of God"</note>

A. An accurate copy of the printed sheet which the Pope gives with the *Agnus Dei*, which is a type of medal made of wax, representing on one side a Lamb, with the inscription: *Agnus Dei qui tollis pecata mundi. miserere nobis. VII*—that is: *Lamb of God! who takes away the sin of the world, have mercy on us.* <note>The Roman numeral VII likely refers to the seventh year of the Pope's reign.</note> as seen at letter B. This medal has, on the reverse side, the image of one or another saint.

C. The coat of arms of Pope Alexander VII, who was the first to issue the aforementioned sheet A; the translation of the sheet can be found here alongside it.

D. The *Scapulars* <term>Scapular: two small pieces of sacred cloth joined by ribbons, worn over the shoulders as a sign of devotion</term>, being two pieces of certain consecrated fabric joined together with ribbons, which are worn under the shirt by most members of religious orders to earn indulgences. (*) one piece has a Latin inscription.

E. A Rosary or Paternoster <note>Latin: "Our Father"</note>, composed of fifteen decades of small beads.

F. An ordinary Rosary decorated with Relics, etc.

G. A ring, which the Knights of Malta use to pray their rosary; the rose upon it turns by means of a spring, and points with a small black dot to the fifteen numbers surrounding it, representing the number of decades or the parts of the rosary mentioned above.

H. A portion or decade of the rosary.

I. Bread of St. Genevieve, being a type of dry biscuit which the monks of St. Genevieve distribute for the healing of fevers. <note>Saint Genevieve is the patron saint of Paris, traditionally invoked against disasters and illness.</note>

K. A consecrated copper medal which the Sisters of Charity wear on their rosary for the preservation of their chastity.

<margin>(*) See Halma, Dictionary, page 945, under the word: *Scapulaire*.</margin>

# The Power of the Agnus Dei.

Composed of holy Ointment, Balsam, and pure wax. An extract from the book named the *Ceremonial*, where, speaking of the consecration of all this, the following words are recorded at the end in this manner.

One reads that Pope Urban V sent three *Agnus Dei* to the Greek Emperor with the following verses and words.

| | |
|---|---|
| It can subdue the power of thunder. | It brings no distress to a mother, |
| It washes away sin purely. | Burdened with cares for her child. |
| Fierce fire shall never penetrate, | When you labor, toil, and struggle, |
| Nor shall water be your grave. | May prosperity be your guarantee |
| It guards you from a sudden death. | Of the enjoyment you aim for. |
| It puts the devils to flight, | Though the object is small in parts, |
| And causes the enemy's plot to fail. | It can heal you of much sorrow. (*) |

## The prayer which the Pope offers at the consecration of the Agnus Dei.

> That it may blot out sin, that forgiveness may be obtained, and that it may grant grace.
> That Christians, when they see and touch it, may be moved to praise God.
> That the noise in the air, hail, snow, storms, the violence of the winds and thunder may be moderated and held back.
> That before the salutary and glorious standard of the cross, which is depicted upon it, the evil spirits may be terrified and flee.
> That he who wears it may have strength against the delusions, deceptions, follies, and craftiness of the devil and of evil spirits.
> That no storm, adversity, pestilential or corrupted air, no falling sickness <term>falling sickness: an archaic term for epilepsy</term>, no torment, storm at sea, no fire, or other inclemency of the weather, may offend, hinder, or harm him who shall devoutly carry it with him.
> That in childbirth the mother and the child may be preserved.
> That all those who wear it may always be in safety, that they fear no danger, that they be not afraid of darkness; that no cruelty of the devil may damage them; that they be not deceived by men; that they be delivered from all danger of fire, of lightning, of storms and tempests; And that women may give birth without the perils of labor, and be delivered from pain and from all danger.

->with the permission of the authorities.<-

PLATE XXIII.

### <term>AGNUS DEI</term><note>Latin for "Lamb of God." These were disks made of wax from the previous year's Paschal candles, blessed by the Pope and distributed to the faithful as protective sacramentals.</note>

# THE VIRTUES OF THE AGNUS DEI

->Composed by Saint Thomas Aquinas, and by the Bishop of Gap, Master<-
->of the <term>Sacred Apostolic Palace</term><note>The official theologian of the Papal household, a role traditionally held by a Dominican friar.</note>, extracted from the History<-
->of Pope Urban V and several other Authors:<-
->collected in the Year of our Lord.<-

---

It should be known that the Pope, in the first year of his Pontificate, and every seven years thereafter, blesses the *Agnus Dei*, which are made of very white, pure, and clean wax, mixed with <term>Balsam</term><note>A fragrant resin representing the "odor of sanctity."</note> and <term>Holy Chrism</term><note>A mixture of oil and balsam consecrated by a bishop, used in sacraments like Baptism and Confirmation.</note>.

The *Agnus Dei* serve:

1. Against lightning, thunder, and all storms of the air.
2. For women who are in labor, to deliver them from all peril.
3. Against fire and conflagrations.
4. Against the dangers of the sea and shipwrecks.
5. To preserve one from sudden death.
6. To drive away evil Spirits and demons.
7. Against the plague, fevers, and other illnesses.
8. To protect against treasons and ambushes.
9. To grant peace and appease seditions.
10. For the remission of sins.

---

->IN ROME, by the Printer of the <term>Apostolic Chamber</term><note>The administrative and financial department of the Papal government.</note>.<-
->1742.<-
->With the permission of the Superiors.<-

# Order of the procession for the canonization of several saints, in the church of Saint Peter, under the Papacy of Clement XI, in 1712.

No. 1. The Abbreviators <note>Officials of the papal court who prepared the first drafts of "briefs" or official letters.</note>
2. The Voters of the Signatura <note>original: "Votans van de geteekende opene brieven." These were high-ranking judges of the Signature of Justice or Grace.</note>
3. The Clerks of the Apostolic Chamber.

5. The Altar Servers carrying the seven candlesticks.
6. The Subdeacon carrying the cross.
7. The Penitentiaries <note>Priests with special authority to hear confessions and grant absolution for serious sins.</note>
8. The Abbots.
9. The Bishops, both active and titular <note>original: "dienende en buiten dienst zijnde," referring to those currently managing a diocese and those holding honorary titles.</note>
10. The Cardinal-Deacons.
11. The Cardinal-Priests.
12. The Cardinal-Bishops.
13. The Legate of Bologna, with the Governor of the Province.
14. The Conservator of the Roman People <note>A high-ranking secular official representing the city administration of Rome.</note>
15. The Grand Constable of the Colonna family <note>original: "hoogste Amptenaar van Colonna." A hereditary title held by the head of the powerful Colonna noble family.</note>
16. The Governor of Rome.
17. The assisting Cardinal-Deacons and the Deacon of the Gospel.
18. The Pope under a canopy carried by the Referendaries <note>The Pope (Clement XI) is shown here in state, shielded by a ceremonial covering.</note>
19. The assisting Chamberlains and the Auditor of the Miter.

# PLATE XXXI.

->THE ESTABLISHMENT of the tithe and the ecclesiastical tax.<-
<note>The "tithe" (*dîme*) was a mandatory contribution, usually ten percent of agricultural produce, given to support the church. The *décime* was a specific tax often levied on the clergy's own income to support the needs of the State or the Papacy.</note>

->RECONCILIATION of the EXCOMMUNICATED person.<-
<note>A ritual of forgiveness where a person previously excluded from the church community is formally welcomed back, often after a period of public penance.</note>

->THE INVESTITURE of a Bishop by the crozier and the ring.<-
<note>Investiture is the ceremony where a new bishop receives the symbols of his spiritual and temporal authority: the crozier (a shepherd’s staff) and the ring (symbolizing his marriage to the Church).</note>

<column-break/>

->DEGRADATION of a BISHOP.<-
<note>Original: *Dégradation*; the ultimate disciplinary act where a high-ranking cleric is formally stripped of his sacred office and reduced to the status of a layperson due to a grave crime.</note>

->THE EXCOMMUNICATION <unclear>of a City</unclear><-
<note>When an entire city was excommunicated, it was known as an "Interdict." During this time, public religious services were suspended, and sacraments were withheld from the entire community to pressure local leaders to repent or submit to church authority.</note>

->DEGRADATION of a HERETIC.<-
<note>A public ceremony in which a person found guilty of heresy—holding beliefs contrary to church doctrine—was stripped of their clerical status or social standing before being handed over to civil authorities for punishment.</note>

# PLATE XLVI.

->THE LYING IN STATE of the late H. I. M. in the State Room.<-
<note>The abbreviation "S. M. I." stands for *Sa Majesté Impériale* (His Imperial Majesty). The "State Room" (Salle de Parade) was the most formal room in a palace, designed for grand ceremonies. Here, the deceased monarch is laid out on a raised platform called a catafalque, surrounded by court mourners and religious symbols of power.</note>

---

->THE OFFERING OF BREAD AND WINE at the MASS FOR THE DEAD.<-
<note>This scene depicts a specific moment in the Requiem Mass. In many historical traditions, the faithful—often the family or designated mourners—would physically bring offerings of bread, wine, or candles to the altar. This was both a symbolic participation in the sacrifice of the Mass and a form of almsgiving for the soul of the departed.</note>

<term>Lying in State</term> <note>original: "Exposition du Corps"</note> — The practice of placing the body of a deceased person of high rank in a public place of honor for viewing and ritual mourning.

<term>State Room</term> <note>original: "Salle de Parade"</note> — A grand apartment in a palace or noble house intended for formal receptions and displays of state, rather than for private use.

<term>H. I. M.</term> <note>original: "S. M. I."</note> — His Imperial Majesty. This likely refers to a member of the Habsburg dynasty, given the "Imperial" title and the 18th-century context of these engravings.

<term>Mass for the Dead</term> <note>original: "Messe des Morts"</note> — Also known as a Requiem Mass, this is a specialized Catholic liturgy celebrated for the peace of the soul of the deceased.

<term>Offering of Bread and Wine</term> <note>original: "Offrande du Pain & du Vin"</note> — A liturgical rite where the elements for the Eucharist are brought forward; in a funeral context, this often included additional symbolic gifts from the community.

### Technical Vocabulary

**BISHOP** <note>original: "évêque"</note>: A high-ranking member of the clergy who holds the fullness of the priesthood and oversees a diocese.

**ASSISTANTS** <note>original: "assistans"</note>: In this context, these are two other bishops who assist the main consecrator during the ceremony.

**OATH** <note>original: "serment"</note>: The solemn pledge made by the candidate to uphold the duties of the office and the teachings of the faith.

**ANOINTED** <note>original: "oint"</note>: To be rubbed or sprinkled with consecrated oil (Chrism) as part of a religious ceremony.

**PASTORAL STAFF** <note>original: "bâton pastoral"</note>: The symbolic crook used by a bishop to represent his authority and care as a spiritual leader.

### Various ways in which the Holy Tribunal <note>Original: *heilige vierschaar*, a historical Dutch term for a court of law</note> causes criminals to be tortured in a subterranean vault.

**A.** The Inquisitor who orders the tortures and who increases, decreases, or stops them as and when he pleases.
**B.** His two assistants with the Secretary.
**C.** A criminal who is being given the torture of water.
**D.** A criminal who is being given the torture of the strappado <note>Original: *wip*, literally "the swing." This involved hoisting the victim by the wrists, which were tied behind their back.</note>.
**E.E.E.** The executioners disguised as ghosts <note>It was common for executioners to wear hoods or robes to remain anonymous and to psychologically terrorize the victim.</note>, who give the strappado to a criminal, which is: that they pull him up to the vault with his hands tied behind his back, and then let him fall toward the ground until his hips are dislocated.
**F.** An elevated bench which can be widened or narrowed as necessary, and upon which the criminal is laid to receive the torture of water; across this device goes a wooden clamp that raises the body of the criminal in the middle, usually breaking the loins and causing unspeakable pain.
**G.** The criminal is filled with water by means of a funnel placed in the mouth.
**H.H.H.** Sergeants of the court, who always keep water ready to fill the funnel.
**I.** Torture by fire, which is performed by stretching the criminal on the ground with their feet against a large fire to roast them until they confess everything one wishes to know from them.
**K.** An executioner who smears the feet of the sufferer with lard <note>Original: *spek*</note> and certain caustic or burning oils to increase his pains and torments.
**D.** <note>Likely a labeling error in the original for L</note> The Physician <term>Medicijnmeester|A medical professional attached to the court</term> of the tribunal, who warns when there is a danger to life.

**A. Arba Kanfot** <note>original: "Arban canfod"</note>, or garment, which the Jews were formerly accustomed to wear and still wear today under their clothing, so as not to be mocked by those among whom they live. <note>This "Four Corners" garment, also known as a *Tallit Katan*, allows the wearer to fulfill the commandment of wearing ritual fringes (tzitzit) discreetly.</note>

> “ hand, that they may be as frontlets between your eyes. And ye shall teach
> “ them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and
> “ when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt write
> “ them upon the door posts of thine house, and upon thy gates.”

### PLATE III.

->(Illustrations of Jewish Ritual Objects)<-

<columns>2</columns>

**A.** **Arba Kanfot** <note>original: "Arbancanfod"</note>. A garment that the Jews wore in former times, and which they now wear beneath their ordinary clothes so as not to offend the customs of the countries where they live. <note>This "four-cornered" garment, also known as a *tallit katan*, allows the wearer to fulfill the commandment of wearing ritual fringes (tzitzit) discreetly while living among non-Jewish populations.</note>
**B.** The **Tzitzit** <note>original: "Sitsith"</note>, or cords, which are attached to the four corners.
**C.** One of these cords shown enlarged with five knots, which symbolize the name of **God**. <note>In Jewish tradition, the combination of knots and windings on the fringe corresponds to the numerical value of the Divine Name.</note>
**D.** **Sabbath Lamp.** <note>A hanging oil lamp, typically with multiple wicks, used to provide light in the home during the Sabbath, as lighting a fire is prohibited once the holy day begins.</note>
**E.** **Unleavened bread** <note>Hebrew: *Matzah*</note> with which they observe the **Passover**. <note>The text likely refers to *Shmura Matzah*, which is "guarded" with extra care from the moment of harvest to ensure no fermentation occurs.</note>
**F.** Ordinary unleavened bread which is eaten during the days of the festival.

<column-break/>

**G.** Branches of **Palm, Willow, and Myrtle**, bound together, which they hold in the left hand; and the **Citron** (marked **H.**) in the right. They bring these together and wave them toward the four winds. <note>These are the "Four Species" used during the festival of *Sukkot* (Feast of Tabernacles). The palm bundle is called a *Lulav* and the citron an *Etrog*.</note>
**I.** **Shofar** <note>original: "Sophar"</note>, or Ram’s horn, which is sounded on the days of the **New Year** <note>Rosh Hashanah</note> and on other festivals.
**K.** A case, or hollow tube, attached to the doorframes of all doors, on the right side, inside of which is enclosed a parchment where are written the passages from the Book of <term>Deuteronomy</term> <note>The fifth book of the Bible</note> chapter 6, verse 4 etc., and chapter 11, verse 13 etc. <note>This is a *Mezuzah*. The verses mentioned contain the *Shema*, the fundamental declaration of Jewish faith: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one."</note>

**Synagogue**: A Jewish house of prayer and assembly.
<note>original: "Synagogue"</note>

**Jews**: Members of the Jewish faith and ethnic community.
<note>original: "Juifs"</note>

**Portuguese**: Refers to the Sephardic Jewish community, many of whom fled the Inquisition in Portugal and Spain to find religious freedom in the Netherlands.
<note>original: "Portugais"</note>

**The Hague**: The administrative capital of the Netherlands, home to a prominent Sephardic community in the 17th and 18th centuries.
<note>original: "La Haye"</note>

<note>original: "Prêtres"</note>

**Aaron**: The brother of Moses; according to biblical tradition, the office of the priesthood is hereditary through his lineage.
<note>original: "Aron"</note>

<note>original: "Bénédiction"</note>

**The People**: The gathered congregation.
<note>original: "Peuple"</note>

<note>original: "Lire"</note>

# The search for the leavened bread

Or the manner in which the leavened bread <note>original: "gedeessemde brood," referring to chametz</note> is gathered together and cleared out of the house. **A.** The mistress of the house who lays some leavened bread here and there, so that her husband, who performs the search, may be able to find something. <note>This refers to the ritual of *Bedikat Chametz*, where crumbs are intentionally hidden so the blessing said before the search is not in vain.</note>

<note>The "Portuguese Jews" refers to the Sephardic community, many of whom fled the Inquisition in Spain and Portugal to find refuge in Amsterdam and other Dutch cities.</note>

Plate 8.

->No. 1.<-

## Simchat Torah, or the Joy of the Law.

**A. The <term>Chatan Bereshit</term> [Groom of Genesis]. B. The <term>Chatan Torah</term> [Groom of the Law]**, both designated as "Grooms of the Law." They represent the kings of *Israel*, who were required on the final day of the <term>Festival of Tabernacles</term> <note>Also known as Sukkot; Simchat Torah marks the end of this festival period.</note> to begin and end the public reading of the Law. The **Chatan Torah** is the individual who finishes the final verses of the Law, and the **Chatan Bereshit** is the one who begins the reading again from the very beginning.
**C.C. Two <term>Parnassim</term> or Elders.** <note>Parnassim (plural of Parnes) were the elected lay leaders or wardens who managed the synagogue's affairs.</note>

->This building represents the Synagogue of the Portuguese Jews in Amsterdam.<- <note>This refers to the "Esnoga," the famous 17th-century Sephardic synagogue in Amsterdam, known for its grand architecture.</note>

---

->No. 2.<-

## The Manner of Escorting the Grooms of the Law Home.

**A. The Chatan Torah**, on the evening of the day he has completed the reading of the law, is escorted to his house by the **Chatan Bereshit**, who walks at his right hand, and by a **Parnassim or Elder**, who walks at his left. They are followed by other **Parnassim, relatives, and friends**, and are protected by several officers of the law. On the day that the **Chatan Bereshit** begins the reading of the Law, the **Chatan Torah** escorts him in turn in the same manner, with the distinction that the **Chatan Bereshit** then occupies the middle position.

Plate 9.

## Tools used for circumcision

1. Small dish upon which the dressings lie <note>original Dutch "pleisters" refers to medicated bandages or plasters used to promote healing</note>.
2. Another dish containing sand, intended for the disposal of the foreskin.
3. Another dressing.
4. Small bottle containing astringent or <term>hemostatic</term> <note>a substance used to stop bleeding</note> powder.
5. The knife used to perform the circumcision.
6. Instrument used to secure the foreskin.
7. Swathe or bandage to hold the dressings in place.
8. Small silver rod over which the foreskin is drawn.

## The Book of the Law

A. A small box containing the names of all the members of the <term>Synagogue</term> <note>a Jewish house of worship and communal study</note>, from which seven persons are chosen by lot to carry and read from the Law. This box is divided into four compartments: the first, marked 1, contains the names of the <term>Levites</term> <note>descendants of the Tribe of Levi who traditionally assist in religious duties</note>; 2 is for placing the names of the Levites after they have read; 3 contains the names of all other members of the Synagogue; 4 is the place for the names of those among the latter group who have already read.
B. <term>Sefer Torah</term> <note>original: "Sepher Tora," meaning the "Book of the Law" or the Five Books of Moses handwritten on parchment</note> or the opened scroll of the Law.
C. The scroll of the Law, closed and bound with a very wide ribbon.
D. The scroll of the Law with its ornaments.
E. The <term>Rimonim</term> <note>original: "Rimonims," literally "pomegranates," referring to the decorative silver finials adorned with small bells</note> or silver ornaments with small bells, which are placed atop the protruding ends of the scroll.
F. Pointer, for the guidance of the one who reads <note>this instrument, known as a "Yad," is used so the reader does not touch the sacred parchment with their hands</note>.

PLATE XIV.

# THE TEMPLE OF MECCA.

A. The Black Stone <term>Black Stone: known in Arabic as al-Hajar al-Aswad, this ancient stone is set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba and is kissed or pointed to by pilgrims</term> embedded in the wall of the Kaaba.

<column-break/>

B. The place where the vestiges of the feet of Abraham <note>Known as the Maqam Ibrahim, this refers to a stone used by Abraham during the construction of the Kaaba, which is said to have miraculously softened to take the imprint of his feet</note> are shown.

<column-break/>

C. The building that contains the well of Zamzam <note>original: "Zemzem"; a sacred spring located near the Kaaba that provided water to Hagar and her son Ishmael in Islamic tradition</note>.
D. The door of the Kaaba.

# The Whirling Ritual of the Dervishes

<insert>God <note>original Arabic: الله (Allah)</note></insert>

<insert>Muhammad <note>original Arabic: محمد</note></insert>

This fine copperplate engraving captures the <term>Sema<note>A sacred Sufi ceremony of the Mevlevi Order, characterized by music, singing, and a rhythmic whirling dance intended to bring the practitioner closer to the Divine.</note></term> in progress. The scene is set within a grand <term>Sema-hane<note>A ceremonial hall or "house of celestial movement" specifically built for the whirling ritual.</note></term>, an architectural space defined by its soaring arches and monumental pillars.

In the center of the hall, a group of <term>Mevlevi<note>An order of Sufis founded in the 13th century by the followers of Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi.</note></term> practitioners perform their spiritual dance. They are clad in long, flowing robes that flare outward as they spin, and they wear the <term>Sikke<note>A tall, conical hat made of felt, which symbolizes the tombstone of the dervish's ego.</note></term>. Their movements are precise and meditative; some stand with arms outstretched to capture the flow of spiritual energy, while others kneel in prayerful contemplation.

The architecture of the hall is richly decorated. Upon the pillars, one can see <term>Levhas<note>Large calligraphic plaques, often displaying the names of God, the Prophet, or sacred verses.</note></term>—represented here by the inscriptions of **God** and **Muhammad**. A large, intricate geometric chandelier is suspended by a long rope from the vaulted ceiling, illuminating the ritual space. Along the right side, a wooden balcony with a decorative balustrade provides a vantage point for musicians and observers, who watch the practitioners move in harmony with the sacred music of the flute and drums.

## Marriage Ceremony of the Turks.

<term>Marriage Ceremony</term> <note>The original Dutch term is *Huwelijks-plegtigheid*, which refers to the formal, ritualistic, and solemn aspects of the wedding celebration, emphasizing the gravity of the legal and religious contract.</note>, <term>Turks</term> <note>In the period this manuscript was produced, "Turks" was a common European label for all subjects of the Ottoman Empire, regardless of their specific ethnic or linguistic background.</note>

*Description of the Illustration:*
This full-page engraving displays a sweeping landscape that combines classical antiquity with contemporary Ottoman life. In the foreground to the left, the wedding procession is led by two figures in long, flowing robes. They carry a large, ornate ceremonial object with seven tiers, which may represent a symbolic crown or a model of a structure signifying the new household. A figure in a tall, peaked hat follows them, gesturing toward the heart of the scene.

The middle ground is dominated by the remnants of the ancient world: a set of massive, broken classical columns—likely of the Corinthian order—stand upon a high, rectangular stone pedestal. As the wedding party passes these ruins, we see a group of figures in traditional turbans and robes. Among them are women whose faces are partially obscured by veils, adhering to the modesty customs of the time.

The background reveals a wide, serene valley featuring a two-story building with a tiled roof, several slender cypress trees, and a body of water. A prominent mountain peak rises in the far distance under a sky of light, drifting clouds. The entire composition is enclosed within a simple border, focusing the viewer’s eye on the intersection of grand history and local tradition.

->PLATE XIX.<-

## TURKISH MARRIAGE.

<note>original: "MARIAGE TURC"</note>

*This engraving depicts a detailed 18th-century scene of an Ottoman wedding procession moving through a picturesque landscape.*

In the foreground, the procession travels from left to right along a dirt path. On the left, several men wearing traditional robes and turbans carry ceremonial objects, including a tall, tiered, and highly decorated structure known as a <term>nahil: a large, tree-like ceremonial ornament decorated with wax flowers, fruits, and gold leaf, symbolizing fertility and the wealth of the families</term>. Following them are more men wearing various styles of Ottoman headwear, indicating their different social ranks.

Towards the right side of the path, the bride is carried in a palanquin <note>also called a litter; a covered chair or bed carried on poles by men or animals</note> enclosed with white curtains to maintain her privacy and modesty. Following the bride is a group of women, some of whom have their faces veiled.

The setting is a picturesque landscape blending nature and history. In the mid-ground, a river flows under a stone bridge with multiple arches. On the left bank of the river stands a large, multi-story building. Dense trees occupy the center of the composition, partially obscuring the view. On the far right, the ruins of three large, fluted classical columns stand on a rectangular stone base, serving as a reminder of the ancient Greek and Roman history that permeates the Ottoman landscape. The background shows rolling hills and mountains under a sky with soft clouds.

**Vocabulary:** Turkish Marriage, Ottoman wedding, procession, palanquin, <term>nahil: ceremonial wax tree</term>, classical ruins, engraving.

# Plate 23.

## A Turkish Cemetery in Constantinople

->[Illustration: A wooded memorial site and burial ground]<-

This copperplate engraving captures the solemn atmosphere of a Turkish cemetery, likely located on the outskirts of <term>Constantinople<note>Modern-day Istanbul.</note></term>. In the foreground on the left, a group of figures is gathered near a tall stone monument or boundary wall. They are dressed in traditional Eastern costume, characterized by long, flowing robes and <term>turbans<note>A distinctive Ottoman headpiece; the specific shape and wrap of a turban often indicated the wearer’s social status or religious office.</note></term>. One individual is seated on the ground in a posture of reflection, looking toward the monument, while others stand nearby in quiet conversation or prayer.

The center of the scene is dominated by a massive, gnarled tree with dense foliage. Its trunk appears split or damaged at the base, a common motif in Romantic-era art to symbolize the passage of time and the cycle of life and death.

To the right, the landscape extends into a sprawling cemetery. Numerous simple grave markers <note>In Ottoman tradition, headstones were often slender marble pillars, sometimes topped with a carved turban for men or flowers for women.</note> are scattered among a grove of smaller trees. In the distance, a solitary figure can be seen standing among the graves, highlighting the vastness and the quiet solitude of the site. The entire composition is framed by a double-line border, typical of high-quality botanical or ethnographic plates of the period.

<summary>This illustration provides a visual representation of the Turkish burial grounds described in the preceding text, showcasing the unique gravestones, foliage, and traditional dress of the Ottoman Empire.</summary>

# Plate 31.

# The Bayram <note>original: "De Bairam"; referring to Eid al-Fitr, the "Lesser Bayram," which marks the end of Ramadan</note>
## or the Easter Festival of the Turks.

On which they engage in all sorts of public amusements; some let themselves be swung through the air, hanging from ropes, others let themselves be spun on a wheel of fortune <note>original: "rad van Avanturen"; likely a reference to a primitive Ferris wheel or a fairground ride</note>, etc. This festival is almost like our ceremonies and amusements at the New Year. But since this festival immediately follows Ramadan <note>original: "Ramadhan"</note>, or the great fast of the Turks, it is compared to the Easter festival <note>the author uses the term "Easter" to help Western readers understand the holiday's significance as a joyful feast following a long period of religious fasting</note>.

<summary>This page describes the celebration of Bayram (Eid al-Fitr), detailing public fairground amusements and comparing the Islamic holiday to European New Year and Easter traditions.</summary>
<keywords>Bayram, Eid al-Fitr, Ramadan, Ottoman customs, Turkish festivals, wheel of fortune, public amusements</keywords>

Plate 32.

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

## The Carnival of the Turks.

This they hold two months before the fast of *Ramadan*, on the first night of the month of *Ramadan* <note>The original Dutch uses "Remesan," likely a phonetic spelling of the month. While the text says two months prior, it specifically refers to the commemorative night of the descent of the Koran.</note>, in memory of the descent of the *Koran* <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> from heaven. The streets are then illuminated and swarm with masked musicians, people on foot and on horseback or seated on camels, and above all a great number of *Santons* or holy men <term>Santons: ascetic wandering monks or dervishes</term>, who were mentioned on Plate 29 No. 4, and who make a terrible noise with their dances, songs, shouts, and howling. In all this crowd appears, seated on a mule, *Sheikh-el-Arfat* <note>original: "Scheï-kel-Arfat"</note>, or prince of the horned ones, who is highly esteemed among the Turks and to whom they give great cheers.

---

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

## The Festival of Hussein in Persia.

At which the deaths of *Hussein* and *Hassan* <note>original: "Hassein"</note>, sons of *Ali* and *Fatima*, who fell in battle, are mourned. Some appear half-naked, painted with blood, and others with black to depict the heat and thirst suffered by *Hussein*; they run together through the streets, bowing and twisting in a hundred ways, making all kinds of distorted facial expressions, and shouting at the top of their lungs: "Hussein! Hassan!" Some dig holes in the ground, bury themselves up to the neck, and remain there the entire day with their heads covered by an earthen pot; others finally appear in military gear to depict the war in which *Hussein* lost his life. A Preacher <term>Prediker: here referring to a religious orator or mullah</term> delivers a eulogy for the saint which lasts two hours, and all these religious ceremonies are followed by the strangest excesses and all kinds of unbridled behavior.

<summary>This page describes two significant Islamic observances: a festive street celebration in the Ottoman Empire marking the revelation of the Koran, and the somber, performative mourning rituals of Muharram in Persia honoring the martyrdom of Hussein.</summary>
<keywords>Islam, Ottoman Empire, Persia, Ramadan, Koran, Hussein, Hassan, religious festivals, Muharram, Santons, rituals</keywords>

# Plate 32: Ceremonial Processions of the East

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

### A Nocturnal Procession through the City

This engraving depicts a nighttime scene set within a bustling Middle Eastern urban environment. A dense crowd of people, many wearing turbans and long, flowing robes, fills the city streets. The darkness of the night is illuminated by several men carrying flaming torches, which cast a dramatic light across the central figures. 

In the heart of the procession, a man dressed in a white robe is guided and accompanied by a dedicated retinue <note>This likely represents the "Sheikh-el-Arfat" or a similar high-ranking official mentioned in the previous text regarding the Turkish Carnival.</note>. To the upper right, observers are seen looking out from the windows of a stone building, watching the formal religious assembly as it moves through the narrow streets. This image captures the vibrant and chaotic atmosphere of the public festivals held during the month of *Ramadan*.

<column-break/>

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

### The Ritual of the Grave

The second engraving illustrates a somber burial scene, likely associated with the mourning rites of the Festival of Hussein. In the center of the foreground, a man is shown bent over his shovel, laboriously digging into the earth to prepare a grave. To his right, a group of figures—including a woman shrouded in a heavy hooded cloak—stand in quiet observation of the work.

The mid-ground is marked by a tall palm tree and traditional stone architecture, under which a larger crowd has gathered. In the distance, a building with a gabled roof and small windows overlooks the site. The composition emphasizes the gravity of the interment ceremony <term>Orientalism: a 17th and 18th-century artistic style where European artists depicted Eastern cultures with a focus on exotic details and dramatic lighting</term>. The scene provides a visual counterpart to the descriptions of participants who, in their grief, would bury themselves as a sign of devotion.

These images serve as visual evidence for the religious customs of the Ottoman and Persian Empires described in the manuscript.</summary>

## The Carnival of the Turks.

They hold this two months before the fast of *Ramadan* <note>original: "Ramadhan"</note>, on the first night of the month of *Remesan* <note>The author may be referring to the start of the three sacred months in the Islamic calendar, or perhaps the Night of Power, though the timing mentioned is unusual</note>, in memory of the descent of the *Quran* <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> from heaven. ## The Festival of Hussein in Persia.

## The CARNIVAL of the TURKS.

They hold this two months before the fast of *Ramadan* <note>original: "Ramadhan"</note>, on the first night of the month of *Remesan* <note>The author may be referring to the start of the three sacred months in the Islamic calendar, or perhaps the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), though the timing mentioned is unusual for a carnival</note>, in memory of the descent of the *Quran* <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> from heaven. The streets are then illuminated and swarm with masked musicians, people on foot and on horseback and seated on camels, and above all a large number of *Santons* <term>Santons: From the Spanish 'santo' (saint); a term used by early European travelers to describe Muslim dervishes or wandering monks</term> or holy men, who were mentioned on Plate 29 No. 4, and who make a terrible noise with their dancing, singing, shouting, and wailing. In all this crowd of people appears, seated on a mule, *Sheikh-al-Arfat* <note>original: "Scheïkel-Arfat"</note>, or prince of the horned, who is much esteemed by the Turks, and to whom they give great cheers.

## The FESTIVAL of HUSSEIN in Persia.

During which the deaths are mourned of *Hussein* and *Hasan* <note>original: "Hassein"</note>, sons of *Ali* and *Fatima* <note>original: "Fatime"</note>, who were killed in battle; some participants appear half-naked, painted with blood, and others with black to depict the heat and the thirst of *Hussein*. They run together through the streets, bowing and turning in a hundred different ways, making all kinds of grimaces <note>literally "ugly facial features"</note>, and shouting at the top of their lungs: "*Hussein! Hasan!*" Some dig holes in the ground, bury themselves there up to the neck, and remain there the entire day, having their heads covered with an earthenware pot; others finally app... <unclear>appear</unclear>

### Technical Vocabulary

*   **Engraving**: A printmaking technique where an image is incised into a metal plate, allowing for fine detail in the illustration.
*   **Ottoman dress**: The distinctive styles of clothing worn within the Ottoman Empire, often signaling rank through the shape of the turban or the quality of the fabric.
*   **Turbans**: Headwear created by winding fabric, used throughout the Islamic world to denote social or religious status.
*   **Architecture**: The structural design of the buildings shown, which blend elements of Eastern styles.
*   **Portico**: A porch or walkway with a roof supported by columns, often serving as a grand entrance to a palace or public building.
*   **Illustration**: A visual representation used to clarify or decorate the accompanying text.

->*SOLAK*<-

**A Solak (Janissary Archer Guard)**
<note>The Solaks were elite archer bodyguards selected from the Janissary corps. Their primary duty was to protect the Sultan during public processions, where they formed a human shield around his horse.</note>

The guard is shown wearing a belted tunic over tight leggings. His most striking feature is a tall, decorative hat adorned with an exceptionally large, fan-like plume. He holds a bow in his left hand and a cluster of arrows in his right.

->*IBRIE-DAR AGA*<-

He is dressed in a long-sleeved robe and a tall conical hat. He carries a large, ornate metal pitcher, or <term>ibrik: a traditional ewer with a handle and spout used for pouring water</term>, which is held within a matching footed basin used to catch the water during the Sultan's washing.

Plate 2

# Brahma or Bruma.

The first of the three principal deities of the East Indians <note>A historical European term for the people of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.</note>; his name signifies: *Wisdom*. The <term>Brahmins</term> <note>The priestly class or varna within Hindu society.</note> attribute to him the creation of all visible and invisible things, humans, and as many worlds as there are parts in his body, from each of which a world has emerged, namely:
    The first, which is above the heavens, from his brain.
    The second from his eyes. The third from his mouth.
    The fourth from his left ear.
    The fifth from his palate and from his tongue.
    The sixth from his heart. The seventh from his belly.
    The eighth from his genitals. The ninth from his left hip.
    The tenth from his knees. The eleventh from his heels.
    The twelfth from the toes of his right foot.
    The thirteenth from the sole of his left foot.
    and the fourteenth from the air and the atmosphere by which *Brahma* 
    is surrounded. <note>This likely refers to the concept of the fourteen "Lokas" or planetary systems in Hindu cosmology.</note>

They further say that there is a great correspondence or mutual affinity between these worlds and the limbs of *Brahma*, in such a way that the people of the different worlds have the same affections and inclinations as are characteristic of the nature of the different limbs of *Brahma*.

<summary>This page describes the Hindu creator god Brahma and a cosmogony wherein fourteen distinct worlds emerged from specific parts of his physical form. It notes that the inhabitants of these worlds inherit the spiritual and natural characteristics associated with those specific limbs.</summary>
<keywords>Brahma, Brahmins, East Indians, creation myth, fourteen worlds, Hindu cosmology, wisdom</keywords>

# Brahma or Bruma.

->**BRAHMA or BRUMA.**<-

The first of the three principal deities of the <term>East Indians</term> <note>A historical term used by early modern Europeans to refer to the people of the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.</note>; his name means: *Wisdom* <note>While the text glosses the name as "Wisdom," the Sanskrit root *brh* typically means "to grow" or "expand."</note>. The first, which is above the heaven, from his brains.
The second from his eyes. The third from his mouth.
The fourth from his left ear.
The fifth from his palate and from his tongue.
The sixth from his heart. The seventh from his belly.
The eighth from his <term>private parts</term> <note>original: "parties honteuses" — a common archaic euphemism for the reproductive organs in early anatomical and ethnographic descriptions.</note>. 
The ninth from his left hip.
The tenth from his knees. 
The eleventh from his heels.
The twelfth from the toes of his right foot.
The thirteenth from his left sole.
And the fourteenth from the air and the atmosphere by which **Brahma** is surrounded.

They say further that there is a great correspondence or mutual attraction between these worlds and the members of **Brahma**, in such a way that the people of the different worlds have the same affections and inclinations as are characteristic of the nature of the various limbs of **Brahma**.

# PLATE I.

<note>This page contains a mirrored ghosting or "bleed-through" from an engraved plate on the opposite side. The following text reflects the corrected reading of the captions as they were intended to be viewed.</note>

->The Second Incarnation.<-
<note>original Latin: "Secunda Incarnatio"</note>

This illustration depicts the **Kurma** or <term>Tortoise avatar</term>. In this foundational myth, a giant tortoise sits at the bottom of the "Ocean of Milk" to support the weight of Mount Mandara. The mountain acts as a churning staff, while groups of deities and demons pull the great serpent Vasuki, wrapped around the peak, to churn the waters and retrieve the nectar of immortality.

->The Fourth Incarnation.<-
<note>original Latin: "Quarta Incarnatio"</note>

Here we see the **Narasimha** or <term>Man-Lion avatar</term>. Having taken a form that is neither purely animal nor purely human, the deity is shown with a lion's head and multiple arms. He is seated in a hilly landscape, disemboweling the demon king Hiranyakashipu across his knees—a specific detail of the legend, as the demon could not be killed by any weapon, nor indoors or outdoors, nor by man or beast.

<column-break/>

->The First Incarnation.<-
<note>original Latin: "Prima Incarnatio"</note>

This scene shows the **Matsya** or <term>Fish avatar</term>. Vishnu is depicted emerging from the mouth of a massive fish in the middle of the primordial sea. He battles the demon Hayagriva to recover the stolen sacred scriptures (the Vedas). In the background, a small boat is visible, representing the vessel used to save the seeds of life from a cosmic flood.

->The Third Incarnation.<-
<note>original Latin: "Tertia Incarnatio"</note>

This depicts the **Varaha** or <term>Boar avatar</term>. The deity, possessing the head of a boar, stands over the defeated demon Hiranyaksha in the ocean. He is shown heroically lifting a sphere that represents the Earth—detailed with tiny buildings and trees—after rescuing it from the depths of the cosmic waters.

<note>The terms used in this plate refer to the first four stages of Vishnu's <term>Dashavatara</term> (the Ten Incarnations): 1. Matsya (Fish), 2. Kurma (Tortoise), 3. Varaha (Boar), and 4. Narasimha (Man-Lion).</note>

<summary>This plate provides a visual catalog of the first four incarnations of the god Vishnu, detailing his zoomorphic and hybrid forms used to preserve the universe in Hindu mythology.</summary>
<keywords>Vishnu, Dashavatara, Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha, Hindu iconography, Avatars, Churning of the Ocean</keywords>

Plate 9.

<insert>No. 1.</insert>

# The Idol Temple of Kamaetsma
## Wife of *Ixora* or *Eswara*; <note>These names are colonial-era Dutch transliterations of "Ishvara," a title for the Hindu god Shiva. Kamaetsma likely refers to the goddess Kamakhya or a local variant of Parvati.</note>

In which, besides various monstrous <note>original: *gedrogtelijke*; this reflects the 18th-century European perspective which often viewed non-Christian religious iconography as "grotesque."</note> displays, the deception of the priests is presented. On the feast day of this goddess, the priests place a child near the fruits that the people offer in abundance, positioned beside a subterranean opening. Then, at the fall of night, they close the doors of the temple and pull the child—along with the fruits and offerings—down through the underground opening to themselves. The following day, they return the child to its original place, decorated with flowers <insert>to suggest a divine miracle has occurred</insert>.

---

<insert>No. 2.</insert>

# The Procession of *Vishnu*,

Or a representation of the idol on horseback, carried upon a plank. He is preceded by torchbearers and covered by parasols <note>original: *zonneschermen*</note> to provide him with shade and to drive away the mosquitoes. For entertainment, a goat or a fox is released, which the Indians <note>In this historical context, "Indians" refers to the Hindu people of the Indian subcontinent.</note> attempt to beat to death with sticks which they hold in their left hands.
