# The Idol Temple of Kamactsma
## Consort of *Ixora* or *Eswara*; <note>The names Ixora and Eswara are early European transcriptions of Ishvara, a title for the Hindu god Shiva. Kamactsma likely refers to the goddess Kamakshi.</note>

In which, besides various monstrous representations, is depicted the deception of the priests. On the feast day of this goddess, the priests place a child alongside the fruits that the people offer in great abundance. This child is positioned next to a subterranean opening; subsequently, at nightfall, the doors of the temple are closed, and the priests pull the child, along with the fruits and offerings, through the subterranean opening to themselves. The following day, they return the child to his place, decorated with flowers. <note>This account reflects common 17th- and 18th-century European travelogues that often characterized non-Christian rituals as "priestly deceptions" to explain the "disappearance" of offerings.</note>

For entertainment, a goat or a fox is let loose, which the Indians <note>The original Dutch *Indianen* refers here to the people of India.</note> attempt to beat to death with sticks which they hold in their left hand.

# PLATE IX.

<meta>N. 1.</meta>

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

->The PAGODA of KAMAKSHI<-
<note>original: "La PAGODE de KAMAETSMA." This likely refers to the goddess Kamakshi, a form of the Great Mother or Parvati, particularly associated with the city of Kanchipuram.</note>

## The Temple of Kamakshi
### Consort of *Ishvara*; <note>The text uses historical transliterations "Ixora" or "Eswara" for Ishvara, a title for the god Shiva.</note>

In this temple, alongside various monstrous representations <note>Early European observers often used "monstrous" to describe multi-armed or non-humanoid depictions of Hindu deities that were unfamiliar to them.</note>, is depicted the alleged deception of the priests. During the feast day of this goddess, the priests place a child near the vast abundance of fruit offered by the people. This child is positioned next to a subterranean opening; as night falls and the temple doors are closed, the priests pull the child, along with the offerings, through the opening to themselves. On the following day, the child is returned to his place, adorned with flowers, to the wonder of the worshippers. <note>This anecdote was a common trope in 17th-century European accounts, intended to portray non-Christian rituals as fraudulent tricks by a "crafty" priesthood.</note>

---

<meta>N. 2.</meta>

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

->The PROCESSION of VISHNU<-
<note>original: "La PROCESSION de WITSNOU." Vishnu is one of the principal deities of Hinduism, the Preserver of the universe.</note>

## The Procession of *Vishnu*

This image shows the idol of the deity on horseback, mounted upon a large platform or plank. The god is preceded by torchbearers and shielded by large sunshades <note>Traditional ceremonial parasols, often called *chhatra*, which signify royal and divine status.</note> intended to provide him with shade and to ward off mosquitoes. For the entertainment of the crowd, a goat or a fox is released, which the local people attempt to strike with sticks held in their left hands.

<term>Pagoda (Pagode)</term>: A term historically used by Europeans to describe both the temple buildings of Asia and sometimes the idols kept within them.
<term>Witsnou/Vistnou</term>: Historical phonetic spellings of the god Vishnu.
<term>Ixora/Eswara</term>: Historical transcriptions of Ishvara, meaning "Lord," usually referring to Shiva in this period's literature.

PLATE XII.

---

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

->The PROCESSION of GANGA.<-
<note>Ganga is the personified goddess of the River Ganges. This illustration depicts a "Ratha Yatra" or chariot festival. The large multi-wheeled vehicle is a *ratha* (ceremonial chariot), and the scene captures the intense devotion of followers, including those performing "prostrations" by lying in the path of the wheels. The right side of the image shows the "Charak Puja," a ritual where participants are suspended from a rotating bamboo pole by hooks pierced through their skin as an act of penance or thanks.</note>

---

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

->The FESTIVAL of HOLI.<-
<note>Original French: "La Fête de Huly." This refers to the Hindu festival of Holi, which marks the end of winter and the beginning of spring. The bonfire shown in the background represents the burning of the demoness Holika. The dancers and musicians in the foreground reflect the joyous, carnivalesque atmosphere of the celebration, which early European observers often compared to their own "Shrove Tuesday" or Carnival traditions.</note>

6. A kind of pit in which a Fakir sequesters himself several times a year, receiving daylight only through a small opening.
7. A Fakir who sleeps supported by a rope. <note>This illustrates a form of extreme austerity where the ascetic avoids the comfort of lying down.</note>
8. Fakirs who remain in this posture their whole lives; women give them food out of charity. <note>These "stationary" penances, such as keeping an arm raised until it withers, were frequently recorded by 18th-century travelers.</note>
9. Several Brahmins whom women invoke and consult as Saints.

12. Fakirs warming themselves.
13. A Fakir who feeds animals out of charity.

Plate 23.

# Magnificent funeral ceremony of the Kings of Tonkin.

<note>Tonkin, referred to here as "Tunquin," was a kingdom in northern Vietnam. These descriptions are typical of 17th and 18th-century European travelogues, which often blended eyewitness accounts with sensationalized reports.</note>

1. Two bailiffs <note>original: "deurwaarders", likely ceremonial ushers or heralds</note> carrying their staves or maces.
2. Twelve officials, pulling forward the catafalque <note>a decorative funeral platform</note> upon which the name of the deceased King is written.
3. Twelve Elephants which the King usually took with him in war.
4. The Master of the Stables and two Pages on horseback, followed by twelve led horses <note>original: "handpaarden", horses led by hand rather than ridden</note>, which sometimes precede the Elephants.
5. The body of the King, drawn by eight deer.
6. The new King and his brothers.
7. The princesses and ladies of state, who carry food for the deceased.
8. The Princes of the Blood, surrounded by musicians <note>original: "speellieden"</note>.
9. Four Governors of the four principal Provinces, carrying bags of gold and incense on their backs.
10. Two wagons with eight horses filled with gold, silk fabrics, etc.
11. A large multitude of the King's officials and the nobility, some on horseback and others on foot, according to their rank and dignity.
A. Galley, upon which the body of the King is placed.
B. Galley, upon which are the Gentlemen who allow themselves to be buried alive with the King. <note>This refers to the practice of ritual accompaniment in death, where courtiers or servants were buried with the monarch.</note>
C. Galley, with the Ladies, who also allow themselves to be buried alive with the King.
D. Two Galleys, carrying the treasures which are buried with the King.

---

This fleet follows the river which flows through the desert, until a very distant and remote place, where the King and all those who choose to keep him company are buried; the secret is not entrusted to anyone except six <term>eunuchs</term> <note>original: "gesnedenen", literally "the cut ones"</note> who are made to swear never to reveal the place of burial.

<summary>This text describes the elaborate funeral procession of a King of Tonkin (Vietnam), detailing the order of the parade including elephants, treasures, and individuals who were to be buried alive with the monarch. Plate 23.

# Magnificent Funeral Ceremony of the Kings of Tonkin <note>“Tunquin” refers to Tonkin, the historic name for northern Vietnam.</note>

1. Two bailiffs <note>original: “deurwaarders,” referring to ushers or ceremonial officers</note> carrying their staffs or clubs.
2. Twelve officials, pulling the ceremonial tomb <note>original: “praalgraf,” a catafalque or decorative hearse</note> on which the name of the deceased King is written.
3. Twelve elephants which the King usually took with him into war.
4. The Grand Master of the Stables and two pages on horseback, followed by twelve led horses, which sometimes precede the elephants.
5. The body of the King, drawn by eight deer. <note>While deer-drawn carriages appear in early European engravings of Tonkin, they likely represent stylized depictions of the region's nobility using local fauna for ceremonial purposes.</note>
6. The new King and his brothers.
7. The princesses and ladies of the court, who carry food for the deceased.
8. The Princes of the blood, surrounded by musicians.
9. Four Governors of the four primary Provinces, carrying bags of gold and incense on their backs.
10. Two wagons with eight horses filled with gold, silk fabrics, etc.
11. A large multitude of the King’s officials, and the nobility, some on horseback and others on foot, according to their rank and dignity.

A. Galley, on which the body of the King is placed.
B. Galley, carrying the Lords who allow themselves to be buried alive with the King. <note>European accounts of this period frequently included sensational claims of voluntary human sacrifice or ritual suicide among courtiers following a monarch's death.</note>
C. Galley, with the Ladies, who also allow themselves to be buried alive with the King.
D. Two Galleys, carrying the treasures which are buried with the King.

This fleet follows the river which flows through the desert, to a very distant and remote place, where the King and all those who choose to keep him company are buried; the secret is not entrusted to anyone but six eunuchs <note>original: “gesnedenen,” literally translated as 'cut ones'</note> who are made to swear never to reveal the place of burial.

<header>Plate 23.</header>

# Magnificent Funeral Rites of the Kings of Tonkin <note>original: "Tunquin"; referring to the northern region of Vietnam during the Lê and Trịnh dynasties.</note>

1. Two bailiffs <note>court officials</note> carrying their staffs or clubs.
2. Twelve officials pulling the catafalque <term>catafalque: a decorated framework or "magnificent tomb" used to support a coffin during a funeral</term> upon which the name of the deceased King is written.
3. Twelve elephants which the King usually took with him into war.
4. The Master of the Horse and two pages on horseback, followed by twelve led-horses <note>spare horses led by hand as a sign of status</note>, which sometimes precede the elephants.
5. The body of the King, drawn by eight deer.
6. The new King and his brothers.
7. The princesses and ladies-in-waiting, who carry food for the deceased.
8. The Princes of the Blood <note>royals related by birth</note>, surrounded by musicians.
9. Four Governors of the four principal provinces, carrying bags of gold and incense on their backs.
10. Two wagons with eight horses, filled with gold, silk fabrics, etc.
11. A great multitude of the King’s officials and the nobility, some on horseback and others on foot, according to their rank and dignity.
A. Galley <note>a large, low ship propelled by oars</note> upon which the body of the King is placed.
B. Galley upon which are the gentlemen who allow themselves to be buried alive with the King.
C. Galley with the ladies who also allow themselves to be buried alive with the King.
D. Two galleys carrying the treasures which are buried with the King.

This fleet follows the river that flows through the wilderness to a very distant and remote place, where they bury the King and all those who choose to keep him company; the secret is not entrusted to anyone except six eunuchs <term>eunuchs: "gesnedenen" in the original Dutch, referring to castrated male officials who held high-trust positions in the palace</term> who are made to swear never to reveal the place of burial.

1. Two bailiffs carrying their staffs or maces.

# *of the Islanders of the MOLUCCAS*.

## *to these ORNAMENTS*.

# PLATE XIV.

# The Gods of the Chinese.

### Taken from the work of Kircher, titled: *China.* <note>Referring to *China Monumentis Illustrata* (1667) by the Jesuit polymath Athanasius Kircher.</note>

# Fo or Fé,

Highest deity among the *Chinese* (of which the name means: *Savior* <note>original: "Zaligmaker"</note>). He is represented with hidden or covered hands, signifying that his power operates all things in an invisible manner. At his sides, he has the two principal reformers of the *Chinese* religion: namely, at his right hand, the philosopher *Confucius* <note>original: "Confutius"</note>, who taught that there is but one single God; and at his left hand *Laozi* <note>original: "Lanzu"</note>, which means "the old philosopher," who likewise recognized and taught nothing other than a single Supreme Being.
D.D.D. are philosophers elevated to the rank of gods.
E. A military commander placed in the rank of gods.
F. A dragon covered with the shell of a tortoise, also representing the god *Fo*. These are the deities of the first rank.
Those of the second rank: C.C.C.H.H. are sons of *Mars* <note>The Roman god of war, used here as a western equivalent for Chinese martial deities.</note>, the god of war, and teachers of that art.
I.K.L.M. Deities of the third rank, set over sublunary <term>sublunary: literally "under the moon," referring to the physical, changing world as opposed to the eternal heavens</term> things, of which one has governance over the water, another over the earth, and another over the fire, etc.

# Quantecong,

Chinese deity, who according to their accounts was their first Emperor. <note>original: "Quantecong"; likely a phonetic rendering of Guan Gong, the deified general Guan Yu. While the text refers to him as the "first Emperor," historical accounts place Guan Yu in the 3rd century AD; early European travelers often conflated legendary heroes with foundational monarchs.</note> They attribute to him the invention of various sciences, the establishment of several useful laws, the introduction of clothing, and of their civil form of government; he also does not appear in the form of an ordinary man, but rather as a hero of miraculous stature and strength. Behind him stands his page Lincheu, a Black man <note>original: "neger"; in historical European depictions of Guan Yu, his loyal attendant Zhou Cang (Lincheu) was often portrayed with very dark skin and a fierce beard, leading Western observers to categorize him using the racial terminology of their time.</note> who was in no way inferior to his master in courage and strength.

<meta>No. 3.</meta>

# A monk, who is punished when he is caught with a woman.

His neck is pierced with a red-hot iron, and a nail is driven straight through this opening, from which hangs a chain ten *Toises* <term>Toise: An old French unit of length equal to approximately 1.95 meters or 6 feet</term> long, which the unfortunate man is obliged to drag through the city until he has collected a certain sum of money for his monastery. Another monk follows him everywhere and gives him lashes with a whip whenever he tries to place his hands on the chain to give himself relief.

# Idolatrous Temple of China.

1. The entrance or great gate of the temple.
2. The wall on both sides provided with large stone or wooden pillars, on which statues of armed giants in Chinese clothing are placed; this wall hides the interior of the temple, so that one can see nothing of what goes on in the temple, even though the gate is open.
3. A large stone vase on which incense burns.
4. The interior or inner part of the temple where the religious practitioners gather.
5. The table before the altar, provided with incense, offerings, and two candlesticks; one also sees there the bamboo <note>original: "Bambou"</note> or the great reed, in which many smaller ones are located, and on which prophecies are to be read; furthermore vases, in which the tools of fate <note>These are likely divination sticks, used in a practice known as *kau chim*.</note> are hidden.
6. The altar of the idols.
7. Two other altars with idols on the right and left sides of the great altar.
8. The religious practitioners, who perform their religious duties.
9. Locations of the pillars on which the roof rests.
10. Two water basins on the right and left side between the forecourts or the front part of the temple and the temple properly so called; fish are kept in them; through these two openings and through the gate alone comes the little light that is in the temple.
11. The location of the two rooms or chapels filled with idols.
12. The tables on the wall of the temple on which the instructions for the ceremonies are found, when the lot is cast.
13. Chinese drum on a table.
14. Chinese bell, hanging on the side of the wall of the temple, of a crude or coarse workmanship upon which a wooden hammer is struck, as also on the large drum five or six times after <insert>the</insert> religious practitioners have finished their prayers before the idols.
15. A bench with holes in which the Mandarins <note>High-ranking officials in Imperial China.</note> and those who are used for processions place their sunscreens <note>Likely ceremonial parasols.</note>, which serve to protect the idols.

# Plate 38

## No. 1. The Great Temple and Palace Terrace

1. The entrance or great gate of the temple.
2. The wall on both sides, supported by large stone or wooden pillars. These pillars hold statues of armed giants dressed in Chinese clothing; this wall serves to screen the interior of the temple, ensuring that the activities within remain hidden from public view even when the gate is open.
3. A large stone vase in which incense is kept burning.
4. The inner part or sanctuary of the temple where the monks and worshippers <note>original: 'godsdienstigen'; referring to the religious community or devotees</note> gather for service.
5. The Table located before the altar, set with incense, offerings, and two candlesticks. Here one also sees the "Bamboo" or large reed container containing many smaller sticks, which are used to read prophecies <note>referring to 'kau chim' or fortune-telling sticks, a common practice in Chinese folk religion</note>, as well as vases containing other instruments of fate.
6. The main altar of the idols.
7. Two secondary altars featuring idols, located to the right and left of the main altar.
8. The worshippers performing their religious duties and ceremonies.
9. The positions of the pillars upon which the roof of the temple rests.
10. Two square water basins or ponds situated to the right and left between the outer courtyards and the temple proper. Fish are kept within them. These two openings, along with the main gate, provide the only light for the temple interior.
11. The location of the two side rooms or chapels <insert>filled with smaller statues and ancestral tablets</insert>.
15. A long bench or ceremonial table used for the preparation of offerings or as a resting place for ritual items.
**A** and **B**. Specific ornamental sections of the expansive paved terrace, showcasing the geometric patterns and decorative square insets of the stone walkway.

Plate 59.

No 1.

# Quack doctors or monks in *China* who occupy themselves with selling wind.

These individuals usually travel in pairs. One of them, with great solemnity, carries a bag on his right shoulder filled with the alleged wind, which he sells for money to those who are naive <note>original: "onnozel" - while it can mean innocent, in this context it refers to being simple-minded or gullible.</note> enough to buy it. These deceivers <term>Kwakzalvers<note>original: "Kwakzalvers." A Dutch term for "quacks" or charlatans who peddled fake remedies and performed street shows.</note></term> usually hold a wooden hammer in their left hand, with which they frequently strike the ground to summon the god or spirit of the wind. According to their claims, this spirit then flies through the air in a human form, seated upon a bird.

---

No 2.

# Religious beggars and *Chinese Quacks*.

These figures ride upon tamed tigers without bit or bridle; they are generally accompanied by religious beggars and penitents who, with a great display of piety, strike their heads against one another.

<note>This passage reflects early European fascinations with Chinese street life, often blurring the lines between actual religious practice and street performance.</note>

# Funeral Procession
### of a High Official
## in China.

The coffin, covered by a <term>canopy<note>original Dutch: "gehemelte," referring to a decorative fabric covering or baldachin used to shade the coffin</note></term>, is preceded by a large number of young men and young women. They carry flowers and figurines of men, women, animals, and so on, which are intended to be burned in honor of the deceased. Behind the coffin, the children of the deceased walk on crutches to demonstrate their grief; the wives of the deceased follow the procession seated in <term>sedan chairs<note>enclosed portable chairs carried by attendants</note></term>, and behind them follow the other relatives and friends.

Plate 42.

->No. 1.<-

## Tidebaïk
### Japanese deity.

Richly decorated with gold and precious stones, she has a boar’s head <note>The description of a boar's head and multiple arms suggests this is Marishiten (Marici), a deity often associated with light and protection in Japanese Buddhism, frequently depicted riding or possessing the features of a boar.</note> crowned with a golden crown set with diamonds, and has four arms, of which one holds a Scepter, the second a flower, the third a dragon’s head, and the fourth a ring. She treads with her feet upon a terrible monster, which may rightly be called the devil. One also sees, as in the following illustration, the various ways of worshipping and offering incense to this idol. The true meaning of this idol is unknown.

<column-break/>

->No. 2.<-

## Amida
### Another deity of Japan.

Who represents the supreme being <note>Amida (Amitābha) is the Buddha of Infinite Light, central to Pure Land Buddhism.</note>; the preservation and liberation of souls from well-deserved punishments is attributed to her <note>While Amida is typically male, early European accounts frequently referred to Buddhist deities using female pronouns based on their graceful appearance.</note>. She appears upon the altar, sitting on a horse with seven heads, and having a dog’s head with a ring in its mouth, to represent the return of time or perhaps eternity; each horse head from the front signifies a thousand centuries. This idol is magnificently decorated with gold and precious stones.

---

->No. 3.<-

## Another representation of the same idol Amida and the manner in which one drowns oneself in her honor.

In the hope of a much richer reward in the paradise of Amida, one places oneself in a small boat, with large stones around the neck, the arms, and the body, and—after having music played for several hours—plunges into the water. Others prepare themselves for this over several days through long speeches on the vanity and nothingness of the world and of all earthly goods. Both allow themselves to be accompanied to the vessel after having enjoyed themselves with their relatives and friends. There are also those who make holes in the bottom of the vessel to drown themselves in that manner, etc. Amida appears here with a female face and with large ear ornaments. In other places, this idol appears in the form of a young man, and sometimes in the form of a man with three heads.

### Kannon, deity of Japan,

According to some reports, the daughter of *Amida* <note>Amida Nyorai, the Buddha of Infinite Light. Plate 44

->Nº 1.<-

## Toranga, deity of Japan,

Who from a Hunter became an Emperor, and after his death, was placed in the rank of the <term>Camis<note>original: "Camis", a Dutch transliteration of *Kami*, the spirits or deities worshipped in Shinto.</note></term> or blessed spirits, and finally in the rank of the gods. He is depicted fighting with an axe against a tyrant, who was supported by eight kings, which is why the tyrant is shown with eight armed arms. Toranga did this during his life, having freed the empire from a feared tyrant, whom he tramples underfoot in the form of a fire-breathing serpent. <note>The figure "Toranga" is a historical European corruption of *Tōshō-daigongen*, the deified name of the Shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu.</note>

<column-break/>

->Nº 2.<-

## Idol-temple of Toranga,

With a square roof, on each corner of which—as on all other <term>Mias<note>original: "Mias", from the Japanese *Miya*, meaning a Shinto shrine.</note></term> or Japanese temples—four gilded oxen are placed. Its walls are decorated with images of the ancient *Camis* or demi-gods.

---

->Nº 3.<-

## Japanese preacher,

On a pulpit almost identical to those in our churches; he has at his side the patron god of his order, to whom offerings are made. From the canopy of the pulpit, lamps are hung; below is the place where the young priests are situated, some sitting and others standing. The preacher is covered by a very large hat like a parasol, and he has a fan in his hand; from time to time he warns the audience to be attentive by striking a bell standing near him. The book from which he takes his subject is a collection of fundamental principles of the doctrine and ethics of his sect. There are travelers who assert that one often hears beautiful pieces of eloquence and piety there.

## Japanese preacher,

->Nº. 1.<-

# The supreme deity who, according to the Japanese, created the world,

He sits, according to the custom of the country, on twelve cushions placed on a large tree trunk, floating in a pond and supported by a turtle. The creator is black as a <note>The original Dutch uses "Moor" and "Negers" to describe the deity's appearance; this reflects historical European artistic conventions where "foreign" or "ancient" deities were often depicted with dark skin and features associated with Africa to denote antiquity or "otherness."</note> Moor, and has a crown on his head that rises to a sharp point; He has a bare chest and has short, thick hair like the Negros. He carries a ring in one of his hands, a scepter in the other, a flower in the third, and a vase in the fourth, from which water flows; all of this undoubtedly has its significance. The idol is gold, as is everything he wears, even the tree trunk, and his clothes are decorated with precious stones. According to the Japanese, this creator drew the first substance of all things from the tree trunk. Two monsters or devils on one side, and three kings on the other—one of whom is a <term>Sin<note>Likely a transliteration of "Shin" or "Kami," terms for Japanese spirits or deities.</note></term> or half-god, and another has four faces, signifying that he has lived for four thousand years—pull together on a snake which is wound twice around the tree trunk to prevent the creation of the world. The sun emerges from the water up to the waist, in the form of a bearded man of middle age; he pricks the turtle with a needle, having his left hand full of these tools.

<column-break/>

->Nº. 2.<-

# Xaca,
### another deity
### of
## Japan,

This is even one of the first, also named <term>Fotoge<note>From the Japanese "Hotoke," meaning Buddha.</note></term>; it is exactly the <term>Xekia<note>A historical transliteration of the Chinese name for Shakyamuni Buddha.</note></term> of the Chinese.

---

->Nº. 3.<-

# The Idol Temple of the Monkeys.

In the middle of which is the large image of a monkey, placed on an altar provided with offerings and a copper basin, which the <term>Bonze<note>A term used by early Western travelers to refer to Buddhist monks.</note></term> or priest strikes with a tool to awaken the devotion of the people, or to remind them of certain duties. On the two sides of this master monkey is a quantity of other monkeys, each on a pedestal, with offerings before them. This entire worship is symbolic and is based on the <term>transmigration of souls<note>The doctrine of reincarnation, central to Buddhist thought.</note></term> or the transition of souls.

Plate 47.

<insert>No. 1.</insert>

# The Idol-Temple of the Bull

The Bull, which one sees here upon a large altar, is made of pure gold, wearing a richly decorated ornament around its neck. It strikes an egg with its horns, which floats in water within a carved rock. By this, the Japanese—as well as other pagans—understand the *Chaos* <note>The state of the universe before the creation of order.</note> from which the world was drawn. By the bull, they signify the Supreme Being, because in the Hebrew language, one of the names for the Ox is also attributed to God. <note>Likely a reference to 'Aleph', the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which originally represented an ox and is associated with 'Elohim' or 'Adonai'.</note>

<column-break/>

<insert>No. 2.</insert>

# The Idol-Temple of the Deity Daibutsu

This temple has a forecourt in which, on both sides, two armed monsters with several arms stand opposite one another. Beyond this forecourt is a large square area with covered walkways, and after this area is another forecourt, decorated with two lions carved from stone, between which one enters the temple. The persons seen on the plate are the Dutch Ambassador with his retinue, accompanied by Japanese officials.

---

<insert>No. 3.</insert>

# Daibutsu, a Japanese Deity

One of the most important of the empire, and as her name implies: the "Great Goddess." <note>original: "de groote godinne." While the <term>Daibutsu</term> (Great Buddha) is typically male, early European accounts often misidentified the gender of Buddhist statues.</note> It is perhaps the same as the *Amida* or the *Buddha* <note>original: "Budhu"</note>, which is to say: the Supreme Being, derived according to some from its specific attributes. The idol sits in the manner of the Easterners upon a low altar-table; she is of an immense stature and rises almost to the vault of the temple. One of her hands has the thickness of a man of average height. She is made of wood that is plastered and covered with gilded copper. Her face and bosom suggest that she is a woman, and her hair is short and thick like that of Africans <note>original: "negers"; a historical reference to the snail-shell curls typical of Buddha statues, which Europeans of the time compared to African hair textures.</note>; she is entirely surrounded by a crown of gilded rays, in which many images of *Kami* <note>original: "Camis"; the spirits or deities of the Shinto religion.</note> are located. To her right and left sides are many other statues, all crowned with rays, much like those of the saints among Christians, and at the foot of the altar are several burning lamps.

# Daibutsu, a Japanese Divinity

One of the most important deities of the empire, and as the name implies: the "Great Goddess." <note>original: "de groote godinne." Although the <term>Daibutsu</term> (Great Buddha) is typically a male representation, early European travelers often misidentified the gender of Buddhist statues based on their graceful features and robes.</note> It is perhaps the same as the *Amida* or the *Buddha* <note>original: "Budhu"</note>, which is to say: the Supreme Being, derived according to some accounts from the ancient traditions of the East. The massive statue is depicted seated in a cross-legged position, bare-chested, with hands held near the lap. A large, radiant halo or mandorla surrounds the figure, filled with numerous smaller celestial beings. Along the sides of the hall, rows of smaller haloed figures stand upon individual pedestals, representing the vast assembly of spiritual protectors.

Plate 48.

# The Temple
->of the<-
## thousand idols
### in *Japan.*

In the center of the temple, the great idol appears in an immense stature, with pierced ears, a bald head, and a shaved chin, like a Brahmin <term>Brahmin: historically, European travelers used this term to describe Buddhist monks or priests, though it specifically refers to the Hindu priestly caste</term>. Above the idol hangs a canopy <note>original: "gehemelte," meaning a ceiling or overhead covering</note> covering five small bells. On the right and left sides of the idol are many images of armed men, dancing Black people <note>original: "negers"; historically used by early European travelers to describe dark-skinned figures or "asuras" found in Buddhist iconography</note>, sorcerers, sorceresses, devils, and even of the winds and lightning. The walls all around are decorated with a thousand idols, crowned, and in every way like Kannon <term>Kannon: (original: "Canon") the Japanese Bodhisattva of Mercy, known for having multiple limbs to help all beings</term>, that is to say, with thirty arms and seven heads on the chest. All the idols and all the ornaments of the temple are made of fine gold. If one were to count all the statues present in the temple, they would far exceed the number of one thousand.

# The Temple

## thousand idols
### in *Japan.*

In the center of the temple, the great idol presents itself, of an immense stature, with pierced ears, a bald head, and a shaven chin, much like a *Brahmin* <note>original: "Bramin." # Kannon <note>original: "Quanwon"; referring to the Bodhisattva of Compassion, Avalokiteśvara, known in Japan as Kannon</note>.

Who, by the number of her arms, corresponds to the idol Puzza <note>original: "Puzza"; an early European transliteration for the Chinese deity Cundī, often depicted with many arms</note>. Two of her arms are raised upward and carry children. Six small children surround the head of Kannon in the shape of a crown of rays. One child appears above the head of Kannon, and another sits upon her very head. The idol rests, like nearly all Japanese deities, upon a <term>Tarate</term> <note>a Dutch rendering of the Sanskrit "utpala" or "padma," referring here to the sacred lotus</note> or sea-flower.

This image is intended to represent the principal manifestation of Amida <note>Amitābha Buddha; in this period, Europeans often conflated Kannon and Amida or saw Kannon as an extension of Amida's power</note>, and that which she has devised for the benefit of the human race. This much is true: the various arms of an idol always indicate the distinct attributes and actions of the divinity represented therein.

<summary>This text describes a Japanese depiction of the deity Kannon, interpreting her many arms and the presence of children as symbols of her divine attributes and her role in human salvation.</summary>

PLATE XLIX.

## KANNON <note>original: "Quanwon"; referring to the Bodhisattva of Compassion, Avalokiteśvara, known in Japan as Kannon</note>.

Based on a Japanese drawing.

Who, by the number of her arms, corresponds to the idol Puzza <note>original: "Puzza"; an early European transliteration for the Chinese deity Cundī, often depicted with many arms</note>. Two of her arms are raised upward and carry children. Six small children surround the head of Kannon in the shape of a crown of rays. One child appears above the head of Kannon, and another sits upon her very head. The idol rests, like nearly all Japanese deities, upon a <term>Tarate</term> <note>a Dutch rendering of the Sanskrit "utpala" or "padma," referring here to the sacred lotus</note> or sea-flower.

This image is intended to represent the principal manifestation of Amida <note>Amitābha Buddha; in this period, Europeans often conflated Kannon and Amida or saw Kannon as an extension of Amida's power</note>, and that which she has devised for the benefit of the human race. This much is true: the various arms of an idol always indicate the distinct attributes and actions of the divinity represented therein.

<summary>This page describes a Japanese depiction of the Bodhisattva Kannon, interpreting her multiple arms and the presence of children as symbols of her mercy and divine role in human salvation.</summary>

# Plate 51.

---

->No. 1.<-

## Darma, a saint of Japan,

The son of an Indian king who, in his life, never had an equal. His existence is placed at the beginning of the sixth century, during which he preached to the Chinese, confirming his teachings with an extraordinarily strict lifestyle. It is said that once, when he allowed himself to be overcome by sleep, he cut off both his eyelids (which is why he is depicted here without eyelids); these were afterwards transformed into two small bushes upon which tea grew, which until that time was unknown. <note>This refers to Bodhidharma, the founder of Zen Buddhism. The legend of his eyelids becoming tea plants is a traditional folk explanation for why tea helps monks stay awake during meditation.</note> This saint is shown standing on a reed in the middle of the water, for according to their account, he traveled across seas and rivers in this manner.

<column-break/>

->No. 2.<-

## Japanese Rosaries or Prayer Beads,

According to the various religious sects of the country.

The first is that of the Jōdo-shū <note>original: "Seodosju", a major sect of Pure Land Buddhism</note> sect.
The second of that of the Zen-shū <note>original: "Sensju"</note>.
The third of that of the Hyakumanben <note>original: "Fiakmanben", referring to the "million repetitions" of prayer</note>.
And the fourth of that of the Ikkō-shū <note>original: "Ikosju", another name for Jōdo Shinshū</note>.
The Japanese and the Chinese count their prayers on them, which are much longer than those of the Christians.

# Biosju,

->No. 1.<-

# Marriage Ceremony in Japan.

The bride and the groom each arrive separately with their relatives outside the city at a certain hill. The groom is followed by wagons full of gifts for the bride's relatives. They climb the hill on stone steps made specifically for this ceremony and place themselves under the tent of the god of marriage. The groom enters from one side and the bride from the other; no one approaches except the closest relatives and the musicians. These musicians place themselves behind the bride, while none stand behind the groom; they remain entirely outside the tent, and the rest of the entourage stays below at the steps. The idol before which the newlyweds stand sits under the tent on an altar; it has a dog's head <note>original: "hondenkop"; this likely refers to a guardian figure or a specific representation of fidelity</note>, signifying the faithfulness they owe each other in the married state. It also holds a cord in its hands to demonstrate the strength and necessity of their mutual union. Between the newlyweds stands the <term>Bonze<gloss>a historical term for a Buddhist monk</gloss></term> or priest who blesses the marriage. At the side of the tent, torches burn, from one of which the bride lights a torch she holds in her hand; while she does this, she repeats the words dictated to her by the priest. She then offers her torch to the groom, who also lights his from it. This being done, the entire entourage breaks into cries of joy and congratulations. A fire is lit at the bottom of the hill into which everything the newlyweds previously used for entertainment is thrown <note>Likely referring to toys or items associated with their childhood or single lives</note>. Others offer them a distaff provided with flax to remind them of the care they must have for the household they are entering. A sacrifice of two bulls for the god of marriage concludes the ceremony, the company returns to the city, and the young woman is escorted to the young man's house.

---

->No. 2.<-

# Funeral Ceremony in Japan.

The procession is led by the <term>Bonzes<gloss>Buddhist monks</gloss></term> or priests, who carry burning torches; they sing and play musical instruments. The closest relatives of the deceased and others walk before the corpse—the men with extinguished torches and the women with veils. Then follows the corpse on a litter, arranged as if on a state bed, in a praying posture. The funeral pyre where they are headed is placed on the ground, covered with a white linen cloth, and surrounded by walls. At the side of the pyre are tables provided with food

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<column-break/>

and braziers in the form of censers. After circling the pyre three times, the corpse is placed upon it while the priests and the relatives call upon its guardian deity. The priest who was at the head of the procession then takes a burning torch, and after touching the head of the deceased with it three times and circling the pyre three times, he throws the torch at the feet of the relatives or the youngest son of the deceased. He picks it up and throws it onto the ground where the pyre is, which is abundantly provided with oil, incense, and other flammable substances; these then catch fire and consume the entire pyre. While the woodpile burns, the relatives fill the censer on one of the tables with incense and fragrant wood and return home; no one remains except some priests and poor people—the former to say their prayers and the latter to eat what is on the tables. The following day, the ashes and bones of the deceased are collected and placed in precious urns, which are buried and covered with copper plates or hewn stones of various shapes. Upon these are inscribed the name of the deceased and the deity they served. People of distinction also have marble statues placed on the graves, on which are engraved the noble deeds or offices of the deceased, as well as their date of birth and that of their death, which corresponds to our ornate tombs and epitaphs. Often, a marble or stone image of the deceased is placed upon it.

Furthermore, the plate also intends to represent the images of two Japanese deities who oversee the dead. One, named *Jene* <note>possibly a transliteration of Enma or Jizō</note>, has four faces and as many arms: in one, he holds a sun; in the second, a floral wreath; in the third, a branch; and with the fourth, he points his finger at a censer. The sun represents divine providence, etc. This deity protects married persons and the elderly. The other deity, named *Xiquani* <note>possibly a transliteration of Shaka (Shakyamuni) or Kannon</note>, oversees souls and young people; she is depicted as a beautiful young woman, but with four arms: in one, she carries a child; in the second, a snake; in the third, a <term>saber<gloss>a curved sword</gloss></term>; and in the fourth, a ring with knots. Her dress is sown with stars. It is not known what the significance is of the parrot she has at her side.

When a great person dies, it often happens that several of their vassals, subjects, and slaves kill themselves to serve their masters in the next world <note>This refers to the practice of *junshi*, or following one's lord in death</note>.

Plate 53.

Nº 1.

# The Festival of Souls in Japan

<note>This refers to the Buddhist festival known as Obon, a time when the spirits of ancestors are believed to return to the world of the living to visit their relatives.</note>

Towards evening, the people go outside the city to speak with the deceased; they bring food to their graves and invite them to come into the city. Convinced that the spirits are coming, the people lead them into the city with burning <term>torches<gloss>translated from 'flambouwen', large ceremonial torches used to light the way for spirits</gloss></term>.

---

Nº 2.

# The manner in which the souls are brought back to their graves on the third evening

They bid the spirits farewell by throwing stones at them—stones which have been gathered from the streets and roads for this purpose—in order to drive them out of the city in this way. For if even a single soul remained behind in the city, it would be considered one of the greatest misfortunes. <note>While the use of stones to "drive out" spirits is a specific observation here, most traditional Obon ceremonies involve "Okuribi" (sending-off fires) or floating lanterns to guide spirits back to the world of the dead peacefully.</note>

<summary>This page describes the Japanese Obon festival, detailing the ritual invitation of ancestral spirits into the city with torches and their subsequent "expulsion" back to their graves on the third night.</summary>
<keywords>Japan, Obon, Festival of Souls, funerary rites, ancestral spirits, torches, folklore, superstition</keywords>

## Stor-junkare, deity of the Laplanders,

These idols are very crudely worked and poorly formed; the first two are made of wood, of which the upper protruding parts represent a human head, and the others are made of stone. Thoron or <term>Thor</term> <note>A variation of the Norse god Thor, adapted into Sámi belief as Horagalles, the thunder god.</note> has a nail in his head, from which a small stone hangs, so that he can strike fire when it pleases him; he stands on a kind of scaffold instead of on an altar, and although this sanctuary looks very little or not at all like a temple, it is nonetheless surrounded by trees and thorn hedges. He is currently the supreme deity of the Laplanders, for they say he is the master of thunder, and they attribute absolute supremacy to him over men and over spirits. The wooden hammer serves him to punish wicked people and devils. <term>Storjunkare</term> <note>Likely from the Norwegian/Swedish 'Store Junker' meaning 'Great Nobleman' or 'Lord.' He was considered a bridge between humanity and the high gods.</note> is a lesser god than Thor, and in a certain sense his deputy; Junkare means: a Governor or deputy. He is the fountainhead from which all the good that men obtain flows. He has also been made a god of the hunt and a protective deity, and every household possesses one.

# Burial Place of the <term>Guebres<note>Historically referred to as 'Gauren' in Dutch; these are the followers of Zoroastrianism.</note></term> or Persians,

Who have preserved their ancient magical religion <note>The original Dutch 'toverkunstige' (magical/sorcery-like) refers to the 'Magi,' the Zoroastrian priestly class from which the word 'magic' originates.</note>, which they derive from Zoroaster. Their burial places are round stone towers, without doors, at a height of thirty-five feet, and ninety feet in diameter <note>original: 'over 't kruis', literally 'across the cross', a traditional measurement for diameter</note>. The corpses are placed upon these towers, a prey to the air and the birds, so that they may be devoured; and when there are more corpses than the space on the tower can contain, they are lowered through an opening which is in the center of the tower, and they are hung from the wall inside; all the bones which remain from the corpses fall into a very deep pit, which is in the base of the tower.

<meta>This translation follows Plate 61 of the Dutch manuscript, describing the religious customs of the "Gauren" (Zoroastrians) in Persia.</meta>

Plate 61.

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

# Marriage Ceremony of the Guebers or Persians.

The newlyweds sit together on a bed. Two *herbads* <note>original: "Hijrbads"; lower-level Zoroastrian priests</note> or priests position themselves before them, one for the Groom and the other for the Bride, having beside them the blood relatives of the newlyweds, their hands [filled] with rice, which is the symbol of fertility. The Groom's priest places his finger on the Bride's forehead and asks her: "Do you wish for the man here present to be your husband?" The Bride's priest does the same to the Groom. Thereupon, the newlyweds give each other their hands. The Groom gives some pieces of gold to the Bride, and those present sprinkle them with rice, while the priests and the next of kin bless them and pray for them. This entire ceremony is performed before the fire <note>A reference to the central role of the sacred fire in Zoroastrianism</note>.

---

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

# The Baptism of the Guebers or Persians by Water and Fire.

After a *dastur* <note>original: "Daroo"; likely a variation of Dastur, a high-ranking priest</note> or cleric has made his prediction concerning the child by consulting the planets of its birth, the Mother gives the child its name; subsequently, it is brought into the temple, where the priest sprinkles it with pure water, which he holds in a vessel made from the bark of the tree called *Hom* <note>original: "Holm"; the sacred Haoma or Hom tree used in rituals</note>, praying to God for the purification of the child; and to sanctify it, he holds it for some time over the fire. When the child has reached seven years of age, it is brought to the temple to be initiated <note>Dutch: "gevormd," referring to a rite of passage similar to confirmation</note>. Two persons hold it over the fire, with the nose and mouth wrapped in a cloth <note>The *padan*, a ritual veil worn by priests and participants to prevent breath from polluting the sacred fire</note> for fear of contaminating this holy element with the breath, and in this position, the child must recite several prayers which the priest has taught it. After this ceremony, the priest gives it water to drink and pomegranate peels to chew, in order to purify it internally as well. He then places it in a water vat and washes its entire body. This being accomplished, the priest clothes it in the *sudra* <note>original: "Soudra"; the sacred undershirt worn by Zoroastrians</note>, being a reddish garment with wide sleeves, and girds it with a wool or goat-hair belt <note>The *kusti*, a sacred girdle</note>, which goes twice around the body and is knotted at the back.

<summary>This page describes two major life-cycle rituals of the Zoroastrian (Gueber) community in Persia: the marriage ceremony and the two-stage initiation/baptism of children involving purification by fire and water.</summary>
<keywords>Zoroastrianism, Persia, marriage rituals, baptism, sacred fire, herbads, sudra, kusti, ritual purification</keywords>

<meta>Nº 1.</meta>

## Marriage Ceremony of the Guebres or Persians

The newlyweds sit together on a bed. Two <term>Hirbads</term> <note>A term for Zoroastrian priests of a specific rank</note> or priests place themselves before them, one for the Bridegroom and the other for the Bride, having beside them the blood relatives of the newlyweds, and their hands filled with rice, which is the symbol of fertility. The priest of the Bridegroom places his finger on the forehead of the Bride and asks her: " *Do you wish the man here present to be your husband?*" The priest of the Bride does the same to the Bridegroom. Thereupon the newlyweds give each other their hands. The Bridegroom gives some pieces of gold to the Bride, and those present sprinkle them with rice, while the priests and the next of kin bless them and pray for them. This entire ceremony is performed before the fire <note>Fire is the most sacred symbol in Zoroastrianism, representing the light of God and ritual purity</note>.

---

<meta>Nº 2.</meta>

## The Baptism of the Guebres or Persians by Water and Fire

After a <term>Daroo</term> <note>An archaic term for a Zoroastrian priest or Dastur</note> or clergyman has made his prediction concerning the child by consulting the planets of its birth, the Mother gives the child a name; subsequently, it is brought into the temple, where the priest sprinkles him with pure water, which he has in a vessel made from the bark of the tree called <term>Holm</term> <note>Referring to the Haoma plant, which is central to Zoroastrian ritual and believed to have healing properties</note>, praying to God for the purification of the child; and to sanctify it, he holds it for some time over the fire. When the child has reached seven years of age, it is brought to the temple to be formed <note>This refers to the initiation ceremony known as the Navjote</note>. Two persons hold it over the fire, with the nose and the mouth bound with a cloth out of fear of polluting this holy element with the breath, and in this posture, the child must recite some prayers which the priest has taught him. After this ceremony, the priest gives him water to drink and pomegranate peels to chew, in order to also purify him internally <note>The pomegranate is highly symbolic in Persian culture, often representing immortality and the fruitfulness of the soul</note>. He then places him in a water vessel and washes his entire body. This being performed, the priest clothes him with the <term>Sudra</term> <note>The sacred shirt, or Sudreh, typically made of white cotton, though described here as reddish</note>, being a reddish garment with wide sleeves, and girds him with a wool or goat-hair belt <note>The Kusti, a sacred cord tied around the waist</note>, which goes twice around the body and is knotted on the back.

<summary>This page describes the ritual life of the Zoroastrian community ("Guebres"), detailing the symbolic use of rice and gold in marriage ceremonies and the dual role of water and fire in childhood initiation rites.</summary>
<keywords>Zoroastrianism, Persian customs, Guebres, marriage rituals, Hirbads, Sudreh, Kusti, sacred fire, Haoma, initiation</keywords>

PLATE LXI.

<meta>Nº 1.</meta>

## Marriage Ceremony of the PARSIS or GUEBRES

<note>original: "Parsis ou Gaures." The term "Gaures" or "Guebres" was historically used by European travelers to describe the Zoroastrian population of Persia.</note>

The newlyweds sit together on a ceremonial bed or raised platform. Two <term>Hirbads</term> <note>A rank of Zoroastrian priest charged with tending the sacred fire</note> or priests place themselves before them—one for the Bridegroom and the other for the Bride. They are accompanied by the blood relatives of the couple, their hands filled with rice, which serves as a traditional symbol of fertility. During the rite, the priest representing the Bridegroom places his finger on the Bride's forehead and asks: "*Do you wish the man here present to be your husband?*" The Bride's priest then asks the same of the Bridegroom. Upon their agreement, the newlyweds join hands. The Bridegroom presents the Bride with pieces of gold, and the gathered witnesses sprinkle them with rice while the priests and next of kin offer blessings and prayers. This entire ceremony is performed in the presence of the fire <note>Fire is the supreme symbol of purity and the presence of the divine in Zoroastrian worship</note>.

---

<meta>Nº 2.</meta>

## * BAPTISM by FIRE of the GUEBRES

After a <term>Daroo</term> <note>An archaic transliteration for a Zoroastrian priest or Dastur</note> or clergyman has provided a prediction for the child by consulting the planets at the time of birth, the Mother grants the child a name. Subsequently, the infant is brought into the temple, where the priest sprinkles them with pure water held in a vessel made from the bark of the tree called <term>Holm</term> <note>Likely referring to the Haoma or a similar ritual plant, believed to possess healing and purifying essences</note>. As the priest prays to God for the purification of the child, he holds the infant for a few moments over the fire to sanctify them. When the child has reached seven years of age, they are brought back to the temple to be formed <note>original: "formé"; in this context, it refers to being formally instructed in the religious law and initiated into the community</note> in the principles of the faith and to receive the sacred vestments.

<summary>This page illustrates the central life-cycle rituals of the Parsi or Zoroastrian community, focusing on the symbolic roles of rice and gold in marriage and the ritual use of water and fire in the purification of infants.</summary>

# Dying Parsi or <term>Guebre</term>, whose soul is received by a dog.

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

# Funerals of the Parsis.

Before giving the corpse as prey to the birds <note>This refers to the practice of excarnation in a Tower of Silence (Dakhma), where bodies are exposed to vultures to avoid contaminating the earth or fire.</note>, it is placed on the ground and a piece of bread is put in its mouth. One of the blood relatives of the deceased brings a dog near the corpse, as close as possible, but without touching the dog; the closer the dog comes to the corpse, the closer (according to their beliefs) the deceased is to salvation. If the dog jumps onto the corpse to take the piece of bread away, it is a certain sign that the deceased is already numbered among the blessed.

After the trial with the dog, two *Daroo's* <note>original: *Daroo's*; likely a phonetic rendering of <term>Dasturs</term>, who are Zoroastrian high priests</note>, standing two hundred paces from the funeral bier, perform a prayer of half an hour in great haste, with their hands piously folded. During this ceremony, the deceased has a piece of paper at each ear which hangs down four finger-widths below the chin. Finally, the corpse is brought to the designated place, and all those present follow behind two by two with folded hands.

<summary>This page describes the funerary rites of the Parsi (Zoroastrian) community, focusing on the "Sagdid" ritual where a dog is used to confirm death and ward off evil spirits, followed by a priestly procession.</summary>
<keywords>Parsis, Zoroastrianism, funeral rites, Sagdid, Dastur, Guebre, burial customs, India, Persia</keywords>

A dog is positioned prominently on the floor near the dying man.* <note>The caption's claim that the dog "receives the soul" is a common 18th-century European misunderstanding of the <term>Sagdid</term> (dog-sight) ritual. In Zoroastrian tradition, a dog—regarded as a spiritually pure creature—is brought to look at the deceased to confirm death and to ward off the *Nasus* (the demon of corpse-pollution).</note>

# NO. 2.

->**FUNERALS of the PARSIS.**<-

*This outdoor scene illustrates the funeral procession. In the foreground, the deceased lies on a wooden bier (stretcher) while the <term>Sagdid</term> ritual is performed once more, bringing a dog close to the head of the corpse. Vultures are seen circling above and perched on the rim of the tower.* <note>The <term>Dakhma</term> was designed for the practice of excarnation. Zoroastrians believe that a corpse is spiritually impure and should not contaminate the sacred elements of earth, fire, or water. By exposing the body to the sun and scavenging birds, the remains are purified and returned to nature.</note>

---

->No. 3.<-

## Execution of punishment of the Guineans.

The criminal is beaten to death with a club, while at the same time a spear is driven through the body from behind; the head is then cut off, which the next of kin take with them to hang on the side of their hut; the body is divided into four parts and the pieces taken away, after which the women mourn the dead.

->No. 3.<-

## Execution of punishment of the Guineans.

The criminal is beaten to death with a club, while at the same time a spear is driven through the body from behind; the head is then cut off, which the next of kin take with them to hang on the side of their hut; the body is divided into four parts and the pieces are carried away, after which the women mourn the dead. <note>This graphic depiction illustrates the severe nature of capital punishment for certain crimes in the historical Kingdom of Guinea as observed by European travelers.</note>

# PLATE LXVI.

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

# Ceremony observed by the **Kaffers** upon the birth of children.
<note>The term "Kaffer" was used by 18th and 19th-century Europeans to describe the Xhosa and other Bantu-speaking peoples of Southern Africa. It is now considered a highly offensive racial slur and is preserved here only to reflect the original historical document.</note>

a. The cleansing of newborn children with cow dung, and exposing them to the air to dry.
b. The abandonment of a child born with any defect; one is simply cast onto the dung heap, and the other is half-buried.
<note>Descriptions of infanticide or abandonment in early colonial literature often reflected European misconceptions or sensationalized accounts of ritual practices intended to protect the community or deal with extreme hardship.</note>

---

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

## The Marriage of the **Kaffers**.

The closest relatives form two circles, one of men and the other of women; the bridegroom is situated in the center of one, and the bride in the center of the other. The person who consecrates the marriage pours water (*) three times over the newlyweds, and then pronounces the blessing in his own manner.

(*) One can see on the plate with what kind of water they are being sprinkled.
<note>European travelers sometimes claimed that ritual "water" used in these ceremonies was actually animal or human urine, often using such details to emphasize the "otherness" of the cultures they were describing.</note>

# Plate 67.

No. 1.

## Religious honors which the Kaffers pay to the moon.
<note>The term "Kaffer" is a historical designation for the Xhosa and other Bantu-speaking peoples of Southern Africa. It is now considered a deeply offensive racial slur; it is preserved here solely to reflect the original 18th-century manuscript for historical study.</note>

This ceremony is celebrated only at the full moon and lasts the entire night with great noise; some dance, scream, and clap their hands, while others gaze at the moon with ecstasy, murmuring or singing unknown words aloud; others cover their faces or hide themselves in caves. This ceremony is often accompanied by other extravagant gestures, such as, for example, throwing oneself to the ground and soon rising again to worship the moon, or calling out loudly: "We greet You, give us milk and honey, increase our cattle," etc., or finally, one person smears the forehead of another with red earth.

---

No. 2.

## Religious honors which the Kaffers pay to a beetle.

Whenever a beetle appears (which they regard as a great blessing for their huts, and as a sign of the forgiveness of their sins), they sing and dance in its honor, and throw around it powder from the herb Buchu *Spiræa* <note>Original: "Spiræa". Buchu refers to plants of the genus *Agathosma*, highly valued for their medicinal and aromatic properties in Southern Africa; *Spiræa* is a Latin botanical classification used by the author to identify the plant type for European readers.</note>; they also sprinkle their huts with it, and they sacrifice two sheep to this insect. If it happens that the beetle lands on one of them, this person is considered a great saint; they sacrifice two sheep to him and slaughter an ox in his honor; with the fat and the intestines of which the saint is smeared and surrounded—the fatty membrane of the intestines is hung around his neck while still quite warm—and he is richly sprinkled with the powder of the Buchu, etc.

<vocab><term>Kaffers</term> (historical term for Southern African Bantu peoples), <term>moon</term>, <term>full moon</term>, <term>beetle</term> (likely a dung beetle or scarab), <term>Buchu</term> (a medicinal aromatic plant), <term>religious honors</term>, <term>ceremony</term>, <term>red earth</term> (ochre)</vocab>

<summary>This page describes two specific spiritual practices: a nocturnal ritual honoring the full moon to ensure prosperity, and the veneration of a beetle as a sacred messenger of forgiveness and luck.</summary>

Plate 68.

No. 1.

## Incorporation of the youths who are accepted into the rank of men.

The entire assembly sits down in a circle, outside of which the one who is to be accepted stands in the same posture. The eldest of the assembly delivers a speech to the group and asks for consent regarding the reception of the youth; having obtained this, he turns to the youth and gives him an admonition regarding the manner in which he must behave henceforth. He then <term>urinates on him</term><note>A practice documented by early colonial observers like Peter Kolbe, who described it as a ritual of purification and blessing among the Khoikhoi, though modern scholars often debate the accuracy or interpretation of these accounts.</note>, which the other undergoes very religiously, carefully smearing his body with this "holy water." The ceremony ends with congratulations and a feast at the expense of the youth, who during this time does not yet dare or is not allowed to eat until after all the others.

On the same plate, *another ceremony* is shown which precedes the aforementioned one; it is that of *reception into civil society*, as among the *Hottentots*<note>original: "Hottentotten." A historical term for the Khoikhoi people, now considered offensive.</note> no one is permitted to enter into marriage unless he has first had a part of his body cut out. To this end, his arms and legs are bound, and the cutter sits upon his belly, opens the place with a sharp knife, removes the piece, fills the wound with a ball of fat and *Buchu*<note>A medicinal plant indigenous to South Africa, known for its healing properties.</note> of equal size, and binds him. During this procedure, some *Hottentots* slaughter a sheep for the meal that follows this ceremony. After the procedure, the entire body of the sufferer is smeared with melted fat, and after the cutter has urinated on him, he is left lying on the ground until he has recovered and is able to crawl to the hut, which has been prepared nearby for this purpose and in which he remains for three or four days. Neither he nor the women are admitted to the feast held on this occasion.

---

No. 2.

## Burial of the *Kaffirs* and *Hottentots*.

The dead body is wound—with the head against the legs—in the hide with which he was covered during his life, and is thus carried on the shoulders to his burial place. The corpse is not carried out through the ordinary door of the hut, but through an opening which is made beforehand toward the side of the field. The entire *Kraal*<note>A term for a traditional African village or cattle enclosure.</note> or company accompanies the corpse in great disorder, making lamentable gestures and letting out a hideous scream. The cavern in which the corpse is placed is carefully closed.

### No. 1 & 2.

## Musical instrument played by the <term>Kaffers</term><note>original: "Kaffers." A historical term used here to refer to the Xhosa or other Bantu-speaking peoples of Southern Africa. In modern contexts, this term is a deeply offensive racial slur; it is preserved here strictly for historical accuracy to the manuscript.</note>.

This is a bow which is strung with a string made of sheep gut; at one end of the string is a <term>quill</term><note>original: "pennen-schagt." This refers to the hollow shaft of a bird feather.</note>, and along the length of the string is a movable device in the form of a small bowl or cup, serving to change and control the tones; this instrument is called: **Gougom.** <note>This instrument is known to musicologists as the *gora*. It is a unique "stringed-wind" instrument where the player produces sound by blowing across a piece of quill attached to the string, which causes the string to vibrate.</note>

### No. 3 & 4.

## Musical instrument played by the women.

This is made in the shape of a pot or kettle drum, covered with a lambskin; it has almost the sound of a drum, and the women play it with their hands and fingers. <note>This likely describes the *khais* or *khu*, a traditional drum often made from a ceramic pot or a hollowed-out wooden vessel.</note>

<meta>No. 1.</meta>

# Burial Ceremony of the Inhabitants of Guinea.

The deceased is buried by the women within his dwelling; the grave into which the body is brought is four or five feet wide, and the body is placed in such a way that the earth does not touch it, for it is surrounded with wood or planks. <note>This practice of lining the grave with wood reflects a desire to protect the remains from the soil, a custom observed by European travelers in various West African coastal regions.</note> Also buried with him are those things which he loved most during his life. The women who bury him process around the grave, which is covered with a roof in the shape of an open hut, making a terrible shouting and wailing; some crawl over the grave, and almost all walk on crutches as a sign of their sorrow. <note>original: "krukken." While translated as crutches, this likely refers to ritual stilts or ceremonial walking staffs used specifically during mourning rites to symbolize the instability or "lameness" caused by grief.</note>

---

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

# The Grave of a King of Guinea.

One places his *fetishes* <term>fetishes</term><note>original: "Fetiches." In 18th-century ethnography, this term referred to objects—such as charms, carvings, or natural items—believed to possess spiritual power or to serve as a dwelling for a spirit.</note> or sacred objects upon his grave, as well as his weapons and everything that is judged he might need. While he is being buried, the people strike dead everyone they encounter—men and women, boys and girls, free people and slaves—so that these might serve the king in the other world; they are killed unexpectedly, their bodies are buried with the king, and their heads are placed on spears around the grave; sentries are also placed there so that no one may come to steal them. <note>These accounts of funerary human sacrifice were frequently highlighted in European texts of this era to emphasize the perceived "barbarism" of foreign kingdoms and to justify colonial or missionary presence.</note>

# Plate 70

---

No. 1.

## Burial Ceremony of the Inhabitants of Guinea.

The deceased is buried by the women within his own dwelling; the grave into which the body is brought is four or five feet wide, and the body is placed in such a way that the earth does not touch it, for it is surrounded with wood or planks. <note>This practice of lining the grave was often highlighted by European travelers to show that these cultures possessed specific "civilized" funeral technologies, such as coffins or wooden casings.</note> Also buried with him are those things which he loved most during his life. The women who bury him process around the grave, which is covered with a roof in the form of an open hut, making a terrible shouting and wailing; some crawl over the grave, and almost all walk on crutches as a sign of their sorrow. <note>original: "krukken." In many West African traditions, ritual stilts or ceremonial staffs were used during mourning to represent the world being "out of balance" or the mourner being unable to walk unaided by grief.</note>

---

No. 2.

## The Tomb of a King of Guinea.

One places his <term>fetishes</term><note>original: "Fetiches." An early modern term used by Europeans to describe objects—such as charms, statues, or natural items—believed by local populations to possess spiritual power or to house a deity.</note> or sacred objects upon his grave, as well as his weapons and everything that is judged he might need. While he is being buried, the people strike dead everyone they encounter—men and women, boys and girls, free people and slaves—so that these might serve the king in the next world; they are killed unexpectedly, their bodies are buried with the king, and their heads are placed on spikes around the grave; sentries are also placed there, so that no one might come to steal them away.

Plate 72.

# The Great Sacrifice of the Inhabitants of *Canada*, to *Quitchi-Manitou*, or the Great Spirit.

<note>original: "Quitchi-Manitou." This is a phonetic Dutch rendering of Gitchi Manitou, a term used by various Algonquian-speaking peoples (such as the Anishinaabe or Cree) to signify the "Great Spirit" or "Great Mystery."</note>

They choose a beautiful day for this purpose, on which they create a large pile of all kinds of valuable merchandise, <note>In the context of the 17th and 18th-century fur trade, "merchandise" would include high-value trade goods like blankets, beads, metal tools, and furs.</note> often reaching the value of forty or fifty thousand crowns, <note>The "crown" (or *kroon*) was a major European currency; forty thousand crowns was an enormous sum, intended to impress the reader with the scale of the spiritual devotion and material sacrifice.</note> which they set on fire and around which there is dancing and singing. Throughout the day, from morning until evening, large tobacco pipes <note>The <term>calumet</term> or ceremonial pipe, used here as a medium to carry prayers to the divine through smoke.</note> are carefully offered toward the sun, etc.

<summary>This text describes a massive ceremonial sacrifice performed by Indigenous peoples in Canada, involving the burning of valuable trade goods and the ritual offering of tobacco pipes to the sun and the Great Spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Canada, Quitchi-Manitou, Great Spirit, sacrifice, trade goods, tobacco pipes, calumet, ritual offering</keywords>

While the preceding page (Plate 73) contained artistic studies after Raphael, this page (Plate 74) resumes the cultural observations of the "peoples of Canada," specifically focusing on their domestic laws regarding marriage and its dissolution.</meta>

Plate 74.
<meta>No. 1.</meta>

# Marriage Ceremony of the Peoples of Canada.

The blood relatives <note>original: "bloedvrienden," literally "blood friends," referring to clan or family kin</note> from both sides gather in the hut of the tribal elders, where they entertain themselves with singing and dancing. The relatives of the bridegroom arrive, with the exception of the four eldest. Meanwhile, the bride arrives at the entrance of the hut with four of her eldest relatives. The elder of the people receives her and has her enter the hut, where he places her on a spread-out carpet <note>likely a woven mat or animal hide</note> beside the bridegroom. They are given a small stick which they hold in their hands for as long as the speech being delivered lasts, after which they break the stick and give the pieces to the witnesses present. Afterward, the newly married woman is brought back to her father's house by her young friends or bridesmaids <note>original: "speel-maagden," or play-maidens</note> who wait for her outside the hut; she remains there and is visited by her husband until she has a child. At that time, she moves to her husband's hut and lives with him for as long as the marriage lasts.

---

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

# Manner in Which the Peoples of Canada Perform a Divorce.

As it would be an unbearable burden for the people of Canada to remain in marriage with the same person for their entire lives, they divorce whenever they please. When this happens, the pieces of the stick mentioned above in No. 1 are brought to the same hut where the <term>betrothal</term> <note>original: "ondertrouw"; the initial marriage agreement</note> took place, and they are solemnly burned there. If the divorce has occurred in proper order and without dispute or quarrel, the children are divided among the divorced parties; when the number is unequal, the mother is given the extra child. This is done so that she might have an advantage over the man, since among the <term>savages</term> <note>original: "wilden"; a common, though now derogatory, historical term used by 18th-century Europeans to describe Indigenous populations</note>, children are considered their treasure and primary wealth.

<summary>This page describes the marriage and divorce customs of Indigenous Canadians, highlighting a ritual involving the breaking and burning of a stick and the matrilineal emphasis on child custody during separation.</summary>
<keywords>Canada, marriage ceremony, divorce, Indigenous customs, kinship, child custody, stick ritual</keywords>

### PLATE LXXIV.

#### No. 1.

->WEDDING CEREMONY of CANADA.<-

The blood relatives <note>original: "bloedvrienden," literally "blood friends," referring to clan or family kin or those bound by the same totem</note> from both sides gather in the hut of the tribal elders, where they entertain themselves with singing and dancing. The relatives of the bridegroom arrive, with the exception of the four eldest. Meanwhile, the bride arrives at the entrance of the hut with four of her eldest relatives. The elder of the people receives her and has her enter the hut, where he places her on a spread-out carpet <note>likely a woven reed mat or a decorative animal hide</note> beside the bridegroom. They are given a small stick which they hold in their hands for as long as the speech being delivered lasts, after which they break the stick and give the pieces to the witnesses present. Afterward, the newly married woman is brought back to her father's house by her young friends or bridesmaids <note>original: "speel-maagden," referring to companions or maidens of the same age</note> who wait for her outside the hut; she remains there and is visited by her husband until she has a child. At that time, she moves to her husband's hut and lives with him for as long as the marriage lasts.

---

#### No. 2.

->THE WAY THE PEOPLES OF CANADA PERFORM DIVORCE.<-

As it would be an unbearable burden for the people of Canada to remain in marriage with the same person for their entire lives if they no longer find happiness, they divorce whenever they please. When this happens, the pieces of the stick mentioned above in No. 1 are brought back to the same hut where the <term>betrothal</term> <note>the formal agreement and ceremony of marriage</note> originally took place. In the presence of the family and witnesses, the pieces of the stick are thrown into the fire <note>this symbolic burning represents the total dissolution of the bond</note>. Once the wood is consumed, the marriage is considered null, and both the man and the woman are free to enter into a new union.
