# Plate 74.

**Canada, Wedding Ceremony, divorce, blood relatives, bridesmaids, betrothal, quarrel**

No. 1.

## Marriage Ceremony of the Peoples of Canada

The blood relatives <note>original: "bloedvrienden," literally "blood friends," referring to clan or family kin</note> from both sides gather in the hut of the tribal elders, where they entertain themselves with singing and dancing; the relatives of the bridegroom arrive, with the exception of the four eldest. Meanwhile, the bride arrives at the entrance of the hut with four of her eldest blood relatives. The elder of the people receives her and has her enter the hut, where he places her on a spread-out carpet <note>likely a woven reed mat or a decorative animal hide</note> beside the bridegroom. They are given a small stick which they hold in their hands for as long as the speech being delivered lasts, after which they break the stick and give the pieces to the witnesses present. Afterward, the newly married woman is brought back to her father's house by her young friends or bridesmaids <note>original: "speelmaagden," referring to companions or maidens of the same age</note> who wait for her outside the hut; she remains there and is visited by her husband until she has a child. At that time, she moves to her husband's hut and lives with him for as long as the marriage lasts.

---

No. 2.

## The Manner in Which the Peoples of Canada Perform Divorce.

Since it would be an unbearable burden for the people of Canada to remain in marriage with the same person for their entire lives, they divorce whenever they please; when this happens, the pieces of the stick mentioned above in No. 1 are brought back to the same hut where the betrothal <note>original: "ondertrouw," referring to the formal agreement or wedding rites</note> took place, and they are solemnly burned there. If the separation is conducted in proper order and without dispute or quarrel <note>original: "krakeel," meaning a noisy or fractious argument</note>, the children are divided between those who have separated, and when the number is uneven, the mother is given one more, so that she may have an advantage over the man; this is because among the indigenous peoples <note>original: "wilden," a term used historically in the 18th century to describe non-European cultures</note>, children are regarded as their treasure and primary wealth.

# Plate 74.

No. 1.

## Wedding Ceremony *of* Canada

The blood relatives <note>original: "bloedvrienden," referring to the clan or kinship group</note> from both sides gather in the hut of the tribal elders, where they entertain themselves with singing and dancing. The relatives of the bridegroom arrive, with the exception of the four eldest members of his family. Meanwhile, the bride arrives at the entrance of the hut accompanied by four of her eldest blood relatives. The elder of the community receives her and leads her into the hut, where he places her on a spread-out carpet <note>likely a woven rush mat or a decorated hide</note> beside the bridegroom. 

They are both given a small, thin wooden rod which they hold in their hands for the duration of the formal speech being delivered. Once the address is finished, they break the stick and give the resulting pieces to the witnesses present to solemnize the contract. Afterward, the newly married woman is escorted back to her father's house by her young friends or bridesmaids <note>original: "speelmaagden," meaning companions or maidens of the same age</note> who have been waiting for her outside. She remains living there, receiving visits from her husband, until she has a child. At that time, she moves to her husband's hut and lives with him for as long as the marriage lasts.

---

No. 2.

## The Manner *in which the* Peoples *of* Canada *perform* Divorce.

Since it would be considered an unbearable burden for the peoples of Canada to remain in a marriage with the same person for their entire lives, they may divorce whenever they please. When this happens, the pieces of the stick <note>referring to the rod broken during the marriage ceremony described in Figure 1</note> are brought back. To signify the dissolution of the bond, these pieces are thrown into the fire in the center of the hut. Following this act, the man typically departs from the common dwelling, gesturing toward the door to indicate his exit from the union, while the woman remains with the children. This is depicted in the scene where a mother holds a swaddled infant while an older child stands at her feet, observing the father's departure.

# PLATE LXXVI.

<note>The term <term>rejoicings</term> (original: *rejouïssances*) was frequently used by early European explorers and missionaries to describe the chanting, dancing, and communal feasts that accompanied the transport of a body. While these appeared "joyous" to outsiders, they were deeply sacred rituals intended to honor the spirit of the departed and provide comfort to the living.</note>

<note>The <term>Cabin of the Dead</term> (original: *Cabane des morts*) refers to a temporary structure where bodies were kept, or perhaps a reference to the large-scale communal burial houses used during the "Feast of the Dead," a significant funerary rite among the Huron-Wendat and other neighboring nations.</note>

Plaat 80.

# The Burial Place
## of the Kings of Virginia.

One skins the corpses as well as one can, cutting away the flesh without damaging the sinews or tendons, so that all the bones remain joined and held in order. One also dries the skeleton in the sun, just as one also preserves the skin in oil or in fat until the dried skeleton is clothed with it; this is done by pulling the skin over the skeleton and filling the empty spaces with sand, so that the corpse appears whole. One then brings it to the burial place, which is a kind of scaffold, inside a reed hut, where the body is laid down and covered. One also dries the cut-off flesh and keeps it in a basket at the feet of the corpse. The idol <term>Kiwasa</term> <note>A wooden deity or protector spirit, often depicted as a seated figure, tasked with guarding the remains of the elite.</note> is placed by the side of the dead to watch over them, and a priest remains there day and night by a fire.

<note>This description and the accompanying illustration are based on the late 16th-century engravings by Theodor de Bry, which were in turn based on the watercolors of John White. They depict an "ossuary" or temple-house used by the Secotan people.</note>

<vocab>Virginia, Kiwasa, burial place, funeral customs, skeleton</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the elaborate taxidermy-like preservation process and the ossuary temple where the bodies of Algonquian kings were kept under the watchful eye of a priest and the deity Kiwasa.</summary>
<keywords>Secotan people, Virginia Algonquians, funerary rites, mummification, Kiwasa, ossuary temple, John White, Theodor de Bry</keywords>

# TOMBS of the Kings of VIRGINIA.

<vocab>TOMBS, Kings, VIRGINIA, burial house, scaffold burial, Indigenous Virginia, Algonquian</vocab>

Plate 80.

# The Burial Place 
## of the Kings of Virginia.

The bodies of the deceased are skinned with great care, removing the flesh while keeping the tendons and sinews intact so that the bones stay connected in their proper order. The skeleton is then dried in the sun, and the skin is preserved with oils or fats. Once the skeleton is prepared, the skin is drawn back over the bones and the interior is filled with fine sand to restore the body’s natural shape, making the corpse appear whole once more. 

The remains are then brought to the burial place, which is a structure of bent reeds resembling a long hut. Inside, the body is laid upon a high wooden scaffold and covered with mats. The flesh that was removed is also dried and kept in a basket placed at the feet of the departed. The idol <term>Kiwasa</term> <note>original: "Kiwasa"; a wooden deity or protector spirit, often depicted as a seated figure, tasked with guarding the remains of the elite.</note> is placed beside the dead to keep watch over them, and a priest remains there day and night, tending a small fire to guard the sanctuary.

<note>This description and the accompanying illustration are based on the late 16th-century engravings by Theodor de Bry, which were in turn based on the watercolors of John White. They depict an "ossuary" or temple-house used by the Secotan people of the mid-Atlantic coast.</note>

<vocab>Virginia, Kiwasa, burial place, funeral customs, skeleton</vocab>

# TOMBS of the Kings of VIRGINIA.

Plate 80.

# The Burial Place 
## of the Kings of Virginia.

The bodies of the deceased are skinned with great care, removing the flesh while keeping the tendons and sinews intact so that the bones stay connected in their proper order <note>This refers to the complex "Quioccosan" burial ritual documented by early explorers like Thomas Harriot and John White</note>. The skeleton is then dried in the sun, and the skin is preserved with oils or fats. Once the skeleton is prepared, the skin is drawn back over the bones and the interior is filled with fine sand to restore the body’s natural shape, making the corpse appear whole once more. 

The remains are then brought to the burial place, which is a structure of bent reeds resembling a long hut. Inside, the body is laid upon a high wooden scaffold and covered with mats. The flesh that was removed is also dried and kept in a basket placed at the feet of the departed. The idol <term>Kiwasa</term> <note>original: "Kiwasa"; a wooden deity or protector spirit, often depicted as a seated figure, tasked with keeping a permanent watch over the remains of the kings.</note>

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic documentation of North American indigenous peoples, transitioning from the funerary rites of the Virginian Algonquians (Plate 80) to the religious ceremonies of the peoples of Florida—specifically the Timucua. This plate illustrates two distinct types of ritual offerings intended to honor the sun and ensure the prosperity of the community.</meta>

Plate 81.

<meta>Nº 1.</meta>

### Sacrifice of the firstborn, which the *Floridians* offer to the sun.

The mother of the child sits bowed before the block, with her face covered, while the other women dance. One of them presents the child to the Prince, whereupon the priest rises from his bench, accepts the child, and crushes it against the block. <note>This chilling scene is based on the 16th-century accounts of Jacques Le Moyne de Morgues. While European chroniclers labeled this as "sacrifice," it is important to note that these accounts were often filtered through a European lens to emphasize the "savagery" of the New World to justify colonization.</note>

---

<meta>Nº 2.</meta>

### Sacrifice of a deer which the *Floridians* offer to the sun.

They take the skin of one of the largest deer they can find and fill it with all types of green herbs, crowning it with wreaths of flowers and fruits. They then place it in this manner upon the top of a tall tree, with its head turned toward the rising sun. The <term>Paraousti</term> <note>original: "Paraousti"; a title for a chief or sovereign among the Timucua people</note> or prince, and the high <term>Jouanas</term> <note>original: "Jouanas"; a term for a shaman or priest</note> or priest, lead the prayers of intercession and guide the singing; on this occasion they pray to the sun for an abundance of fruits and for the fertility of their fields.

PLATE 82

No. 1.

## Ceremony observed by the Kings of *Florida* before undertaking a war expedition.

The King implores the sun to be favorable to him, takes water in a wooden bowl, and throws it toward the sun in such a manner that a portion of it falls upon the soldiers who surround him, saying to them: "*May you shed the blood of your enemies in this manner!*" After this, he fills the bowl with water once more and throws it into the fire burning beside him, saying to his soldiers: "*May you thus exterminate your enemies, just as I extinguish this fire!*" <note>This ritual is a classic example of "sympathetic magic," where a physical act—splashing water like blood or dousing a flame—is performed to ensure a similar result occurs in reality. The sun was the central deity for the Timucua people described in these accounts.</note> This ceremony is accompanied by horrible screaming and frantic gestures.

---

No. 2.

## A King of *Florida* consulting his sorcerer before marching against the enemy.

<note>The term "sorcerer" (original: *tovenaar*) refers to a shaman or spiritual leader. In 16th-century European accounts, these figures were often depicted as having direct communication with spirits or the environment to predict the movement of enemies or the outcome of battles. In the accompanying artwork for this text, the shaman is typically shown in a distorted or trance-like state during the consultation.</note>

<summary>This page details the martial rituals of the Timucua people, specifically how leaders used elemental symbols of water and fire to bless soldiers and consulted spiritual advisors to predict the outcome of war.</summary>

## One of the KINGS of FLORIDA, consulting his MAGICIAN, before marching against the Enemy.

The king and his warriors wait in silence, treating the shaman's visions as divine military intelligence.

Plate 84.

# The Manner of Burying the Kings and Priests of *Florida*.

The grave is surrounded by arrows which are stuck into the ground. The drinking-bowl of the prince <note>In this context, "prince" refers to the *cacique* or chief of a Timucua community.</note> is placed upon the grave. People weep and fast by the grave for three consecutive days, and above all, this is done by the professional mourners <note>original: "klaagvrouwen"; these were women specifically designated to lead public displays of grief.</note> three times a day; the princes of the lineage attend this. Everything that the deceased possessed during his life is burned. The same is also done at the burial of the priests: they are buried in their own dwellings, and the entire property of the deceased is set on fire. <note>The destruction of a leader's property served both a spiritual purpose—sending the items to the afterlife—and a social one, preventing the accumulation of dynastic wealth and ensuring the new leader started fresh.</note>

<summary>This text details the high-status funerary customs of the Timucua people, including the use of symbolic grave markers, ritual fasting, and the ceremonial burning of a leader's or priest's earthly possessions.</summary>
<keywords>Timucua, Florida, burial customs, indigenous chiefs, priests, mourning rituals, funerary architecture, ritual burning</keywords>

### PLATE LXXXIV.

->The Manner of Burying the KINGS and PRIESTS of FLORIDA.<-

# Manner of the Kings
# and Priests of *Florida*
## for burial.

The grave is surrounded with arrows, which are stuck into the ground. The drinking-bowl of the prince <note>Dutch: *prins*. In this context, it refers to the sovereign chief or *Cacique* of the Timucua people.</note> is placed upon the grave. Everything that the deceased possessed during his life is burned. ## Huitzilopochtli. <note>original: *Vitzliputzli* — An early European phonetic spelling of Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec god of war and the sun.</note>

Under this name, the *Mexicans* recognized their supreme deity. He is shown in human form, seated on an azure stone <note>Likely referring to turquoise, a stone of immense sacred value in Aztec culture.</note> throne, which was placed upon a portable sphere. The carrying poles ran straight through this sphere and were decorated at both ends with snake heads; by these, the priests carried the idol in procession from time to time. He wore a helmet on his head in the shape of a bird of various colors with a gilded beak. His face was engraved. He had two blue marks on his forehead and beneath his nose; his right hand rested on a snake, and in his left he held four arrows and a shield upon which five white feathers were placed in the shape of a cross. Everything had its meaning. The sphere, for example, signified the infinite power of the gods; otherwise, this idol was entirely surrounded by curtains.

# PLATE LXXXVII.

<meta>N.1.</meta>

->Captive flayed after having been defeated.<-

<note>This illustration depicts the ritual flaying of a prisoner of war. In Aztec religious practice, particularly during the festival of *Tlacaxipehualiztli*, victims were sacrificed and their skin removed. This skin was then worn by priests or devotees to represent the renewal of the earth—symbolizing the "husking" of a seed to allow new growth—a practice dedicated to the deity Xipe Totec, "Our Lord the Flayed One."</note>

<column-break/>

<meta>N.2.</meta>

->Captive fighting against a MEXICAN Priest.<-

<note>This scene shows a form of ritual combat known as gladiatorial sacrifice or *Tlahuahuanaliztli*. The captive, often a high-ranking warrior from a rival city-state, was tethered by one leg to a large circular stone called a *temalacatl*. To make the fight uneven, the captive was usually given mock weapons—such as a club decorated with feathers instead of sharp obsidian blades—while his opponents, like the priest shown here in his feathered crown and cape, were fully armed. If a captive managed to defeat several opponents in succession, they might occasionally be spared, though most ultimately met their end on the stone.</note>

<column-break/>

<meta>N.3.</meta>

->The Great Temple of HUITZILOPOCHTLI in the City of MEXICO.<-
<note>original: "Vitsliputsli"</note>

<note>This panoramic view displays the *Templo Mayor*, the architectural and spiritual heart of the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan <term>Tenochtitlan: the ancient name for the city now known as Mexico City</term>. The temple was a massive stepped pyramid topped by two distinct shrines: one dedicated to Huitzilopochtli, the god of war and the sun, and the other to Tlaloc, the god of rain. The engraving highlights the vast walled precinct that surrounded the pyramid, which was large enough to contain an entire neighborhood of houses, as well as the dense urban grid and surrounding mountains that characterized the island city.</note>

PLATE LXXXVIII.

<meta>No. 1.</meta>

# Mexican Penitents.

Incense was offered to the idol while several musicians summoned the people together by blowing upon horns. Each worshiper began their penance by making an incision in their heel using a stone tool <note>likely a blade made of obsidian, a sharp volcanic glass</note>, continuing until they had gathered enough blood to smear upon their bodies and to moisten a portion of the temple. Afterward, they went to wash themselves in a river. Other forms of penance were performed by the priests, acting as mediators between God and men; these consisted of some scourging themselves in the presence of the god of penance, *Tescalipuca* <note>original: "Tescalipuca"; this refers to Tezcatlipoca, the "Smoking Mirror," a major deity associated with judgment, night, and fate</note>, using whips made of knotted cords, while others bruised one another with stones.

---

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

# Sacrifice of the Prisoners.

The victims were led to a repository of skulls, which was a scaffold supported by beams <term>Tzompantli: a wooden rack or palisade used to publically display the skulls of sacrificial victims</term>. There, the prisoners were forced to wait at the foot of the scaffold under the guard of Mexican soldiers until they were summoned to be slaughtered, having no comfort other than the sight of thousands upon thousands of fleshless heads. Subsequently, a priest would come to present them with an idol made of flour and honey <note>these were often images made of *tzoalli*, a dough of ground amaranth seeds mixed with honey or agave sap, which was sometimes eaten ceremonially</note>. After the priest withdrew, the victims were led onto the scaffold. Six priests seized the unfortunate soul and stretched him out upon a stone, carved in the shape of a wooden horse's back <note>this describes the *techcatl*, a sacrificial stone usually designed with a convex top to arch the victim's chest upward, making the incision easier</note>. Two held him by the feet, two by the arms, the fifth supported the head, and the sixth, being the sacrificer, opened his chest, cut out the heart, and displayed it while still steaming to the sun; turning then toward the idol, he threw the heart before its face. This being done, the body was cast down the steps to the bottom of the scaffold.

# PLATE LXXXVIII.

## No. 1.

->MEXICAN PENANCES.<-

Incense was offered to the idol while several musicians summoned the people together by blowing upon horns. Each worshiper began their penance by making an incision in their heel using a stone tool <note>likely a blade made of obsidian, a sharp volcanic glass used for its extreme sharpness</note>, continuing until they had gathered enough blood to smear upon their bodies and to moisten a portion of the temple. Afterward, they went to wash themselves in a river. Other forms of penance were performed by the priests, acting as mediators between God and men; these consisted of some scourging themselves in the presence of the god of penance, *Tescalipuca* <note>original: "Tescalipuca"; this refers to Tezcatlipoca, the "Smoking Mirror," a major deity associated with judgment, night, and fate</note>, using whips made of knotted cords, while others bruised one another with stones.

---

## No. 2.

->SACRIFICE OF THE CAPTIVES.<-

The victims were led to a repository of skulls, which was a scaffold supported by beams <term>Tzompantli: a wooden rack or palisade used to publicly display the skulls of sacrificial victims</term>. There, the prisoners were forced to wait at the foot of the scaffold under the guard of Mexican soldiers until they were summoned to be slaughtered, having no comfort other than the sight of thousands upon thousands of fleshless heads. Subsequently, a priest would come to present them with an idol made of flour and honey <note>these were often images made of *tzoalli*, a dough of ground amaranth seeds mixed with honey or agave sap, which was sometimes eaten ceremonially in a practice called "eating the god"</note>. After the priest withdrew, the victims were led onto the scaffold. Six priests <note>original: "Six prie..."</note> performed the final rite: four held the victim by the arms and legs, a fifth held the throat, while the sixth opened the breast with a flint knife to tear out the heart and offer it to the sun.

Plate 89.

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

# The **Mercury** <note>The author uses "Mercury," the Roman god of commerce and travel, as a comparative figure to help European readers understand the role of the Mexican deity.</note> of the **Mexicans**, as he was formerly worshipped at **Cholula** under the name of **Quetzalcoatl**. <note>original: "Quetzalcouati"</note>

It was especially the merchants who paid their respects to him. Forty days before the festival of this deity, a slave of good stature was purchased who, during that time, represented this deity, and for whom he finally had to be killed; he was honored all that time as a god, and many offerings were made to him; he spent that time dancing and enjoying himself, lacking nothing, and people enjoyed themselves with him, even until the very end of the last day, but at the exact minute he was slaughtered, and his dead body cast down to the bottom of the temple. <note>This ritual refers to the concept of the *ixiptla*, where a human being became the living embodiment of a god before sacrifice.</note>

---

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

# The deity who presides over the hunt. <note>This likely refers to Mixcoatl, the god of the hunt and the Chichimec people.</note>

This [deity] was a great lover of the hunt during his life; therefore, divine honors were paid to him through solemn hunting parties. The idol <term>afgod</term> <note>literally "off-god" or idol; a term often used by European writers of this period to describe non-Christian deities.</note> was placed on an altar at the top of a mountain. The religious hunters lit fires at some distance from the idol and hunted wild animals which, to avoid the fire, moved toward the top of the mountain, where the hunters finished them off with arrows, javelins, and clubs before the idol, sacrificing to him the hearts of the killed animals.

PLATE LXXXIX. No. 1.

### The **Mercury** <note>The author uses "Mercury," the Roman god of commerce and travel, as a comparative figure to help European readers understand the role of the Mexican deity Quetzalcoatl as a patron of trade.</note> of the **Mexicans**, worshipped at **Cholula** under the name of **Quetzalcoatl**. <note>original: "Quetzalcoatl"</note>

It was especially the merchants who paid their respects to him. Forty days before the festival of this deity, a slave of good stature was purchased who, during that time, represented the god himself. For this period, he was honored as a living deity and received many offerings. He spent his days dancing and enjoying every luxury, lacking for nothing, and the people celebrated with him until the very final moments of the last day. At the appointed minute, he was sacrificed, and his body was cast down from the top of the temple. <note>This ritual describes the concept of the *ixiptla*, a Nahuatl term for a person who becomes the "image" or living embodiment of a god before being sacrificed to renew the deity's power.</note>

---

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

### **Deity** who presides over the **Hunt**. <note>This deity is likely Mixcoatl, the "Cloud Serpent," who was the patron of hunting and the Chichimec people.</note>

This deity was said to be a great lover of the hunt during his earthly life; therefore, divine honors were paid to him through solemn hunting ceremonies. The <term>idol</term> <note>The original uses the term *afgod*, a Germanic word meaning "false god" or idol, reflecting the European perspective of the era.</note> was placed upon an altar at the summit of a mountain. The religious hunters would light fires at some distance from the image to drive the wild animals toward the peak. To escape the flames, the beasts would flee toward the top of the mountain, where the hunters waited to finish them off with arrows and javelins.

<summary>This page illustrates two significant aspects of Mexican religious life: the merchant-led worship of Quetzalcoatl involving human personification, and a mountain-top ritual dedicated to the god of the hunt.</summary>

### Every 28 years, everything becomes equal again. <note>This refers to the Solar Cycle of the Julian calendar, a 28-year cycle after which the days of the week fall on the same dates of the month.</note>

<image-desc>A grid of dots is arranged here in seven columns and four rows, totaling twenty-eight positions. This visualizes the 28-year solar cycle mentioned in the heading. In the original manuscript, a faint circular bleed-through from the other side of the page is visible, showing a mirrored diagram of a clock or calendar.</image-desc>

One can also find this arrangement of an entire year applied to an individual month, for the arrangement of 13 weeks—representing the four quarters of a year—comprised 365 days. <note>The author is calculating the year by dividing the 52 weeks of a year into four "quarters" of 13 weeks each.</note> The <term>year-name</term> <note>original: "jaars-naem"</note> was the <term>month-letter</term> <note>original: "maands-letter"</note> assigned to the Sundays of the month, and so the month-letter continued to determine the position of the day until the 31st day. And if the month began on Monday, the <term>year-letter</term> <note>The "year-letter" or Dominical Letter is a device used in the Christian calendar to find the day of the week for any given date.</note> fell on the 13th day; and if the month began on Tuesday, the 12th day; and if the month began on Wednesday, the 11th day, and so forth.

Furthermore, there is yet another arrangement here, but as it only extends to Sunday, we shall leave it at that, since one can find the remainder of the arrangement on **Plate 95**.

# Plate 90.

# Mexican century, or figurative representation of a century and a year among the Mexicans.

They made their ideas known and expressed their thoughts about visible things through metaphors or symbols in the manner of the ancient Egyptians; <note>The author compares Mexican pictograms to Egyptian hieroglyphs, a common practice in 18th and 19th-century scholarship to help European readers understand non-Western writing systems.</note> their centuries and years were represented in this way: A painted wheel contained the span of a century, divided into years and provided with memorable events. The century consisted of fifty-two solar years, each of 365 days. Four periods of 13 years each formed the division of the wheel and corresponded to the four parts of the world <note>The four cardinal directions: North, South, East, and West.</note> in the following way: A serpent surrounded this wheel and indicated the four divisions by its four knots. The symbol of the first, which indicated the south, was a Rabbit on a blue background, which was called <term>Tochtlila</term> <note>original: "Tochtlila"; likely a corruption of the Nahuatl *Tochtli*, meaning rabbit.</note>. The second for the east, [represented] by a Staff or cane on a red background; they called this <term>Acatl</term> <note>Nahuatl for "Reed."</note>. The third for the north, [represented] by a dagger with a stone point on a yellow background, and was named <term>Tecpatl</term> <note>Nahuatl for "Flint" or "Stone Knife."</note>. The fourth for the west, [represented] by a house on a green background, named <term>Calli</term> <note>Nahuatl for "House."</note>. Between these four divisions there were another 12 small ones, in which the four symbols were successively divided, each giving its numerical value up to 13, which was the number of years that formed the period; the same took place in the second, third, and fourth periods with the same names from 1 to 13, until the circle of 52 years was completed, in the following manner:

<image-desc>A triangular arrangement of small circles or dots, organized into thirteen horizontal rows. The first row contains one circle, the second row contains two circles, and each subsequent row increases by one until the thirteenth row, which contains thirteen circles. The circles are left-aligned, creating a stepped right-angled triangle shape.</image-desc>

This counting by 13 was observed not only for the years but also for the months. They renewed their count when they reached 13. The solar year consisted of 365 days, and the months of 20. The names and the symbols of the months are depicted by No. 1, 2, 3, and so on up to 18. To complete the year of 365 days, the Mexicans added 5 days to the 18 months (each of 20 days), and this then constituted the year. <note>These five extra days were known as the *Nemontemi*, considered unlucky or "empty" days by the Aztecs.</note>

---

### PLATE XC. NO. 1.

The Mexicans explained their thoughts and gave form to physical objects through Hieroglyphs, in the manner of the ancient Egyptians. <note>18th-century scholars frequently used the term "hieroglyphs" to describe any pictographic or ideographic writing system they encountered, drawing a direct parallel between Mexican codices and Egyptian inscriptions.</note> It is in this manner that their Century and their year were represented. A painted wheel contained the span of a Century, distinguished by years and filled with memorable events. The Century consisted of 52 Solar Years, each of 365 days; 4 Indictions <note>A term borrowed from Roman chronology to describe a recurring cycle of years—in this case, the 13-year segments of the Aztec 52-year cycle.</note> of 13 years each formed the division of the wheel and corresponded to the 4 parts of the World in the following manner.

A Serpent surrounded this wheel, marking the 4 divisions with its 4 knots. The Hieroglyph for the first, which marked the South, was a Rabbit on a blue background, which they called <term>Tochtli</term> <note>Nahuatl for "Rabbit."</note>; for the second, the East, a reed on a red background, called <term>Acatl</term> <note>Nahuatl for "Reed."</note>; for the third, the North, a sword with a stone point on a yellow background, called <term>Tecpatl</term> <note>Nahuatl for "Flint" or "Flint Knife."</note>; for the fourth, the West, a house on a green background, called <term>Calli</term> <note>Nahuatl for "House."</note>. Between these four divisions, there were twelve small spaces in which the four Hieroglyphs were distributed successively, giving to each its numerical value up to 13, which was the number of years that composed the Indiction. They did the same in the second indiction, with the same names from one up to 13, and in the third and fourth until

<column-break/>

the Circle of 52 years was finished, in the following manner:

Plate 91.

<insert>No. 1.</insert>

## Despair of the Mexicans at the end of a century.

Since they believed that at the end of one century <note>The "century" mentioned here refers to the Aztec "Calendar Round," a 52-year cycle. The Aztecs believed the world could end at the conclusion of any such cycle if the sun failed to rise.</note> or another the end of the world would come, they regularly prepared themselves for death on the last day of every century. They broke all their pottery, as useless for the future; they extinguished all their fires, and ran like madmen through the streets, until the dawn began to break. Afterwards, they kept their eyes fixed toward the east, and when the sun rose, they greeted it with all their musical instruments and shouts of joy; one congratulated the other, because they could at least—as far as the existence of the world was concerned—rely on another century again. They went to the temples to thank the gods, and to receive "new fire" from the hands of the priests, which the priests made on the altars by rubbing two pieces of hard wood against each other. <note>This is the "New Fire Ceremony" (Xiuhmolpilli). The fire was started in the chest cavity of a sacrificed victim and then distributed by torchbearers to restart every hearth in the region.</note> After this, everyone set about finding other household items and new pottery, and this day was designated for all kinds of amusements and public displays of joy, as is shown on this plate under No. 2.

Plate 92.
<meta>No. 1.</meta>

## Marriage of the Mexicans.

The priest tied the end of the groom's cloak <note>Likely the 'tilma', a traditional rectangular garment worn by men.</note> and that of the bride's head-veil together, to represent the union of their wills; in this attire, he accompanied them to their home. <note>This ritual of physically tying the garments together is a well-documented centerpiece of Aztec weddings, symbolizing the creation of a new social bond.</note>

---

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

## Ceremony Which the Mexicans Observe With Respect to Their Children.

The children were brought to the temple, and the priests spoke to them regarding the miseries of this life. <note>Central to Aztec philosophy was the idea that the earth was a place of sorrow and trial, and children were often warned of this immediately following birth.</note> If they were the children of nobles, they were given a sword in the right hand and a small shield in the left—items with which the priests were always provided for this ceremony. If they were the children of artisans or craftsmen, the ceremony was performed with certain tools of their art or profession. To the girls, they gave <term>distaffs and bobbins</term><note>Spinning and weaving were sacred tasks for women in Aztec society, and these tools symbolized their future domestic and economic contributions.</note>, after the manner of the Africans <note>original: "Afrikanen." Early European historians often compared the indigenous peoples of the Americas to those of Africa to help their readers understand unfamiliar customs.</note>. Afterward, the priest brought the child before the altar, where he made several incisions on the ears and the genitals with a certain thorn or a stone lancet <note>These lancets were typically made of obsidian, a sharp volcanic glass used in many ritual bloodletting ceremonies.</note>. Finally, they poured water over them and washed them, accompanied by a magical incantation. <note>Many Spanish observers interpreted this ritual washing as a "heathen" version of Christian baptism.</note>

Plate 93.

# Burial of the Mexicans.

At the site of the funeral pyre or grave, all the household goods and weapons of the deceased were brought; and if they were great lords, much gold and silver was included to be burned or buried with them. Some of their servants were killed, as well as their chaplains <note>The author uses the European term "kapellanen" to describe indigenous priests or spiritual attendants.</note> and court jesters, to keep them company in the next world; even their lawful wives usually climbed upon the pyre and allowed themselves to be burned with the corpses of their husbands.

Plate 94.

No. 1.

## Idols of Campeche and Yucatan.

Previously, one saw here a kind of platform <note>original: "tooneel" – in this context, it refers to a raised stone dais or sacrificial stage</note>, made of hewn stones, four ells <note>An "ell" (el) was a historical unit of measurement; in the Netherlands, it was roughly 27 inches or 69 centimeters</note> high and filled with earth; on one side of this platform appeared a human figure made of marble; two hideous monsters seemed to want to tear it apart. On the other side was the image of a serpent, 47 feet long and thick in proportion, which was swallowing a lion <note>While the text says "leeuw" (lion), this likely refers to a jaguar, the large feline native to the region</note>; near and upon the serpent, one saw a number of bodies of murdered men stretched out (as it was presumed to be the custom of the peoples of these regions); this is all that is known of these images, which undoubtedly had their own significance.

---

No. 2.

## Idols of Tabasco.

They opened the chests of human victims and cut out the heart. The bleeding body was then placed upon the neck of a marble **lion**, in which there was an opening through which the blood flowed into a stone drainage basin <note>original: "verlaatbak" – a reservoir or sluice-like container for collecting liquid</note> situated beneath the head of the lion. A human figure, standing opposite the lion by the drainage basin, seemed to very attentively observe the blood flowing into it. And as for the heart, the priest <term>bestreek</term> <note>anointed or smeared</note> the face of the idol with it, and subsequently threw it into the fire that burned at the side of the idol.

# Plate 94.

<meta>No. 1.</meta>

## ->IDOLS of CAMPECHE and YUCATAN.<-

Previously, one saw here a kind of platform <note>original: "tooneel" – in this context, it refers to a raised stone dais or sacrificial stage</note>, constructed from hewn stones. It stood four ells <note>An "ell" (el) was a historical unit of measurement; in the Netherlands, it was roughly 27 inches or 69 centimeters</note> high and was filled with earth. On one side of this platform appeared a human figure carved from marble, which two hideous monsters seemed to be attempting to tear apart. 

On the opposite side was the image of a serpent, 47 feet long and of proportional thickness, which was depicted swallowing a lion <note>While the text says "leeuw" (lion), this likely refers to a jaguar, the large feline native to the region</note>. Near and upon the serpent, one could see several bodies of murdered men stretched out, as it was presumed to be the custom of the peoples of these regions. This is the extent of what is known regarding these images, which undoubtedly held significant local meaning.

---

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

## ->IDOLS of TABASCO.<-

In these rituals, they opened the chests of human victims and cut out the heart. The bleeding body was then placed upon the neck of a marble **lion**, which contained an opening through which the blood flowed into a stone drainage basin <note>original: "verlaatbak" – a reservoir or sluice-like container for collecting liquid</note> situated beneath the head of the lion. 

A human figure, standing opposite the lion by the drainage basin, appeared to very attentively observe the blood as it flowed into it. Regarding the heart, the priest <term>anointed</term> <note>original: "bestreek" – to smear or apply a substance, such as blood, over a surface</note> the face of the idol with it, and subsequently threw it into the fire that burned at the side.

# Plate 95.

**Nº 1.**

# Marriage of the Panama Indians.

Following the engagement, which takes place without much ceremony, they immediately proceed to the formal betrothal <term>ondertrouw: a traditional Dutch term for the formal registration of intent to marry, here used to describe the indigenous ceremony of commitment</term>. Those who are invited to the wedding bring all sorts of gifts, such as axes, stone knives, poultry, fruit, cotton, etc. At the entrance of the hut, the Groom offers each of the guests a bottle of *Chicali* <note>original: "Chicali"; likely a variant of "chicha," a fermented beverage made from maize or fruit common throughout Central and South America</note>, which is the common drink of the land. Everyone drinks of it, even the children; then the fathers of the newlyweds enter, each leading their child—the one his son, the other his daughter—by the hand. The father of the Groom delivers a speech to the assembly, armed with his bow and an arrow, the point of which he offers <note>This gesture likely symbolizes his protection of the new household or a peaceful surrender of his son to a new state of life</note>. Afterward, he dances with extraordinary gestures until he is sweating and can no more out of fatigue; the father of the Bride does the same on his part. After the dance, they both kneel down across from one another and, in this posture, mutually offer their children to each other while holding them by the hand. When this ceremony is finished, the companion <note>original: "speelnoot"; literally 'playmate,' used here to denote the best man or a ritual attendant</note> of the Groom goes with his followers, provided with axes, to the trees that must serve for the construction of the hut for the newlyweds. They chop them down, assemble the hut, level the ground around it, and prepare it; and as the men prepare the ground, the women sow it under the supervision or guidance of the Bride’s companion <note>the bridesmaid or female ritual attendant</note>. Only after eight days is the Bride given to the Groom.

---

**Nº 2.**

## The manner in which friends and blood relatives prepare the ground, intended for the newlyweds, to be cultivated.

# PLATE 95. NO. 1.

-># WEDDING of the INDIANS of PANAMA.<-

Following the engagement, which takes place without much ceremony, they immediately proceed to the formal betrothal <term>intent to marry: originally "ondertrouw," a traditional Dutch term for the formal registration of a couple's plan to wed, applied here to indigenous customs</term>. Those who are invited to the wedding bring all sorts of gifts, such as axes, stone knives, poultry, fruit, cotton, etc. At the entrance of the hut, the Groom offers each of the guests a bottle of *Chicali* <note>original: "Chicali"; likely a variant of "chicha," a fermented beverage made from maize or fruit common throughout Central and South America</note>, which is the common drink of the land. Everyone drinks of it, even the children; then the fathers of the newlyweds enter, each leading their child—the one his son, the other his daughter—by the hand. 

The father of the Groom delivers a speech to the assembly, armed with his bow and an arrow, the point of which he offers <note>This gesture likely symbolizes his protection of the new household or a ritualistic surrender of his authority over his son to a new state of life</note>. Afterward, he dances with extraordinary gestures until he is sweating and can do no more out of fatigue; the father of the Bride does the same on his part. After the dance, they both kneel down across from one another and, in this posture, mutually offer their children to each other while holding them by the hand. When this ceremony is finished, the companion <note>original: "speelnoot"; literally 'playmate,' used here to denote the best man or a ritual attendant</note> of the Groom goes with his followers, provided with axes, to begin the physical labor that secures the couple's future.

<meta>N.2.</meta>

-># RELATIVES and FRIENDS CLEARING the LAND destined for the NEWLYWEDS.<-

In this second scene, we observe the communal nature of indigenous life in Panama. Marriage is not merely a contract between two individuals, but a social event that requires the active participation of the entire village. To support the new couple, the male relatives and friends gather to perform the arduous task of clearing the forest <term>land clearing: the process of removing trees and brush to prepare a field for planting</term>. 

Using tools such as axes and ropes, they fell trees and clear the dense vegetation to create a plot of land where the husband can plant crops to sustain his new family. While some men labor at the trees, others use hoes to turn the earth. In the background, the festive atmosphere continues near the thatched dwellings, where music and dancing signify the joy of the community in welcoming a new household. This practice ensures that the newlyweds have the means to provide for themselves from the very start of their union.

## Plate 96.

# The Manner in Which Caribbean Priests Inspire Courage.

The ceremony <note>original: *plegtigheid*; refers to a formal or solemn ritual</note> begins with singing and dancing until everyone foams at the mouth and behaves like one possessed. A little while later, they calm down and sing and dance in a more orderly fashion in a circle.

All those who ask for the "spirit of courage" (as they call it) take one another by the hand and continue dancing, while three or four priests enter the circle. One priest carries a bottle on a small stick, and the others are provided with reeds filled with burning tobacco <note>Tobacco was considered a sacred plant by many indigenous Caribbean groups, such as the Kalinago, and its smoke was believed to carry prayers or impart spiritual strength</note>. They blow the smoke from this tobacco onto the dancers, saying to them: "Receive, all of you, the spirit of bravery <note>original: *dapperheid*</note> through which you shall overcome your enemies!"

<summary>This text describes a ritual performed by Caribbean priests intended to instill bravery in warriors through trance-like dancing and the ceremonial blowing of tobacco smoke.</summary>

<keywords>Caribbean, priests, ritual, tobacco, courage, indigenous ceremonies, dancing, spiritual possession</keywords>

->The Manner in which CARIBBEAN PRIESTS blow Courage.<-

The ceremony <note>original: *cérémonie*; refers to a formal or solemn ritual</note> begins with singing and dancing until everyone foams at the mouth and behaves like one possessed. A little while later, they calm down and sing and dance in a more orderly fashion in a circle.

All those who ask for the "spirit of courage" (as they call it) take one another by the hand and continue dancing, while three or four priests <note>original: *prêtres*</note> enter the circle. One priest carries a bottle on a small stick, and the others are provided with reeds filled with burning tobacco <note>Tobacco was considered a sacred plant by many indigenous Caribbean groups, such as the Kalinago, and its smoke was believed to carry prayers or impart spiritual strength</note>. They blow the smoke from this tobacco onto the dancers, saying to them: "Receive, all of you, the spirit of bravery <note>original: *courage*</note> through which you shall overcome your enemies!"

# Plate 97.

<insert>
No 1.

## The manner in which the indigenous people of Paria treat their sick.

They submerge the person who has a fever <note>original: *koorts*</note> in a river, and then chase him with blows from sticks around a large fire until he can hardly catch his breath, after which they bring him into the hut to let him sleep. <note>The original Dutch uses the term *wilden* (savages), a typical colonial designation for the Indigenous populations of the Americas.</note>
</insert>

<insert>
No 2.

## Dance of the indigenous people of Paria around the dying, and their burial ceremonies.

Accompanied by mournful songs and wailing with which they perform the burial, they provide the deceased with provisions <note>original: *levensmiddelen*; food and supplies intended for use in the afterlife</note>, which they bury along with them.
</insert>

<term>Paria</term> — A region in modern-day Venezuela (the Paria Peninsula) where early European explorers, including Christopher Columbus, first encountered the Indigenous peoples of the South American mainland.

Plate 98.

No. 1.

## Funeral ceremonies of the peoples who inhabit the surroundings of the **Orinoco** river.

After the flesh of the bodies has been consumed by worms, they hang the skeletons from the planks of their huts and decorate them with feathers and necklaces. <note>This practice of secondary burial involves allowing the body to decompose naturally before cleaning and displaying the bones as a form of ancestral veneration.</note>

---

No. 2.

## Funeral ceremonies of the **Brazilians**.

Here one sees on one side a **Boïe** <term>Boïe: a term for a shaman or spiritual leader, often acting as a bridge between the physical and spirit worlds</term> or priest, who is also a master of medicine, visiting a sick person in his bed or hammock, holding in his hand his **Maraca** <note>original: *Maraque*</note>, which is a type of gourd-fruit in the shape of an ostrich egg. <note>These rattles were sacred instruments used in healing and summoning spirits.</note> On the other side, one sees the manner in which the dead are brought to the grave; they are wrapped in a cotton sheet, and if it is an adult <note>original: *groote*, literally "a great one"</note>, in his own bedsheet. They bury them standing in a round and deep hole, dug into the earth in the manner of a well. The **Brazilians** mourn their dead, making sorrowful gestures, etc.

<header>Plate 99.</header>

<insert>
<margin>No. 1.</margin>
## **The Inca** (as the Kings of Peru were previously called) **offering his vase to the sun.**

This is performed in the magnificent and rich temple of the sun in *Cusco* <note>The Coricancha, or "Golden House," which was the most important temple in the Inca Empire</note>, whose four walls were covered with beaten gold; the image of the sun, positioned above a great altar, extended from one wall to the other, and its rays overlapped one another. On either side of the sun, one saw the bodies of their deceased kings, seated on golden thrones, with their faces bowed toward the earth and so artfully embalmed <note>These were the *mallquis*, or royal mummies, which were treated as if they were still living, brought out for public ceremonies and consulted for advice</note> that one would have taken them for living people.
</insert>

<insert>
<margin>No. 2.</margin>
## **The Inca receiving the offerings which his subjects make to the sun.**

Several of the principal subjects appeared masked, some among others with wings, just as angels are depicted; they also decorated themselves with the actual wings of the bird called the **Cuntur** <term>Cuntur: the Dutch rendering of the Quechua word *Kuntur*, known in English as the Andean Condor; it was a sacred bird believed to be a messenger between the living world and the heavens</term>.
</insert>

# Plate 100.

<insert>
->No. 1.<-

## Method by which the *Peruvians* ignite the sacred fire on the day before the Festival of the Sun, called the great *Rami*.
<note>original: "Rami". This is a Dutch transcription of the Quechua term "Raymi," specifically referring to *Inti Raymi*, the Festival of the Sun, which remains the most important religious ceremony in the Andean highlands.</note>

They had (so they said) to receive the fire from the sun itself for the offerings which they made to it. They then took a large bracelet to which a vessel was attached, about the size of an orange, extraordinarily polished and brilliant. This was held against the sun in such a way that its rays were gathered into a single point upon a tuft of cotton (used in place of other combustible materials), which quite naturally caught hold and was set ablaze. <note>The author is describing the use of a concave mirror or "burning glass" to focus solar energy, a sophisticated scientific practice used by the Inca to symbolize the Sun's direct participation in the ritual.</note> With this fire, they burned all their offerings on this day and prepared the food they intended to consume.
</insert>

<insert>
->No. 2.<-

## The *Inca* offers the Sun a vessel with a pleasant drink and invites the Sun to drink, on the first day of the great Festival of the Sun.
<note>The "pleasant drink" mentioned here is <term>chicha<gloss>A fermented maize beer that was central to Andean social and religious life.</gloss></term></note>
</insert>

<summary>This page describes two central rituals of the Inti Raymi festival: the technological method of igniting a "sacred fire" using a solar mirror and the ritual offering of maize beer to the Sun deity.</summary>

Plate 102.

<insert>
<margin>No. 1.</margin>

## Sorrow of the Peruvians at the time of a Lunar Eclipse.

Because they believed that the moon was now angry with them, or sick, they feared that she would die and fall down upon them. <note>The Incas and other Andean peoples interpreted a lunar eclipse as a "sick moon" or a moon being attacked by a celestial mountain lion (puma) or serpent.</note> To prevent this misfortune, they made a terrible noise and shouted loudly, blowing on horns and trumpets, and beating on kettledrums. They also tied dogs to trees and whipped them to make them howl, in order to wake the moon—whom they believed lay in a faint and particularly loved dogs—and bring her back to herself. <note>Early chronicles suggest the Peruvians believed the moon was sensitive to the cries of dogs, which were thought to have a special spiritual connection to the lunar deity.</note>
</insert>

---

<insert>
<margin>No. 2.</margin>

## A prisoner sacrificed by the Antis or Antipodes.
<note>The "Antis" refers to the ethnic groups living in the Antisuyu, the eastern part of the Incan Empire bordering the Amazon. European writers often used the term "Antipodes" to refer to people living on the opposite side of the globe, but here it likely serves as a phonetic or conceptual confusion with "Antis."</note>

This happened only to prisoners of high rank; they were bound to a large stake or to a tree, and with razors and stone knives, piece after piece was cut from his body, which the men, women, and children ate before the eyes of the unfortunate man while he was still alive, moistening themselves with his blood. <note>Accounts of ritual cannibalism among the Antis were common in Spanish colonial chronicles, such as those by Garcilaso de la Vega, though modern historians often view these as exaggerated to justify "civilizing" missions.</note> The mothers also moistened the nipples of their breasts with it, so that the children would suck in the blood along with the mother’s milk. Those who endured this cruel torture with steadfastness were placed in the rank of the gods after their death, and their skeletons were hung in a hut on the height of a mountain; those, on the contrary, who underwent it with impatience <note>original: "ongeduld"; implying a lack of stoicism or bravery under torture.</note> were thrown onto the dung heap.
</insert>

Plate 103.

<insert>
<margin>No. 1.</margin>

## Manner in which the *Incas* unite those of their kinship in marriage.

There were certain periods in which the king gathered together everyone from his kinship <note>original: "maagschap," referring to the extended royal family or clan known as the *ayllu*</note> who had reached a marriageable age; he would then place himself in their midst and call upon this person and that person, whom he wished to have united in marriage, and made them promise mutual fidelity to each other.
</insert>

<insert>
<margin>No. 2.</margin>

## Manner in which the sons of the *Incas* had their hair cut and were given a name.

When the children were two years old, the entire kinship gathered before the king. The godfather <note>original: "peter," a Dutch term for a male sponsor or godfather used here to describe a traditional Inca ritual role</note>, chosen for this ceremony, began by cutting some hair from the child with a well-sharpened stone razor, and was supported or helped in this ceremony by the child's blood relatives, each according to their rank, until all the hair was cut; immediately after this ceremony, they gave the child a name according to their custom, and placed the gifts they wished to give before him; all this was followed by a feast and a dance, and the festivities <note>original: "vermakelijkheden," literally "amusements" or "pleasures"</note> were sometimes repeated for several days in succession.
</insert>

# The manner in which the *Inca* joins those of his kinship in marriage.

There were certain periods at which the king gathered all those of his kinship <note>original: *maagschap*, referring to the royal *ayllu* or extended family group</note> who had reached marriageable age; he then placed himself in their midst, called those whom he wished to have joined in marriage, and had them pledge their mutual loyalty to one another.
</insert>

---

<insert>
No. 2.

# The manner in which the hair is cut and the name is given to the sons of the *Incas*.

When the children were two years old, the entire kinship gathered before the king. The godfather <note>original: *peter*. In the Andean tradition of the *rutuchikuy* ceremony, this was a high-ranking ritual sponsor</note>, chosen for this ceremony, began by cutting some hair from the child with a well-sharpened stone razor <note>usually made of obsidian or flint</note>, and was supported or assisted in this ceremony by the child’s blood relatives, each according to their rank, until all the hair was cut off; immediately after this ceremony, they gave the name to the child according to their custom and placed the gifts they wished to give before him; all this was followed by a banquet and a dance, and the festivities were sometimes repeated for several days in succession.
</insert>

Plate 103.

<insert>No. 1.</insert>

## The manner in which the *Inca* joins those of his kinship in marriage.

There were certain periods during which the king gathered all those of his kinship <note>Dutch: *maagschap*; referring to the *panacas* or royal lineage groups</note> who had reached marriageable age. He then placed himself in their midst, called forward those whom he wished to have joined in marriage, and had them pledge their mutual loyalty to one another.

---

<insert>No. 2.</insert>

## The manner in which the hair of the sons of the *Incas* is cut and they are given a name.

When the children were two years old, the entire kinship gathered before the king. The godfather <note>Dutch: *peter*; in the Andean context, this was a high-ranking ritual sponsor</note>, chosen for this ceremony, began by cutting some hair from the child with a well-sharpened stone razor <note>usually made of obsidian</note>, and he was supported or assisted in this ceremony by the child’s blood relatives, each according to their rank, until all the hair was cut off. Immediately after this ceremony, they gave the name to the child according to their custom and placed the gifts they wished to give before him. All of this was followed by a banquet and a dance, and the festivities were sometimes repeated for several days in succession.

PLATE 103. No. 1.

->THE MANNER in which THE INCA <note>original: "L'YNCAS"</note> marries THOSE of his BLOOD.<-

There were certain periods during which the king gathered all those of his kinship <note>Dutch: *maagschap*; referring to the *panacas* or royal lineage groups</note> who had reached marriageable age. He then placed himself in their midst, called forward those whom he wished to have joined in marriage, and had them pledge their mutual loyalty to one another.

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

->They CUT the HAIR, and give a NAME to the SONS of THE INCA.<-

<note>This ritual is known as the *Rutuchikuy*, a major milestone in the life of an Incan child marking their transition from infancy.</note>

When the children were two years old, the entire kinship gathered before the king. The godfather <note>Dutch: *peter*; in the Andean context, this was a high-ranking ritual sponsor</note>, chosen for this ceremony, began by cutting some hair from the child with a well-sharpened stone razor <note>usually made of obsidian</note>, and he was supported or assisted in this ceremony by the child’s blood relatives, each according to their rank, until all the hair was cut off. Immediately after this ceremony, they gave the name to the child according to their custom and placed the gifts they wished to give before him. All of this was followed by a banquet and a dance, and the festivities were sometimes repeated for several days in succession.

Plate 104.

<margin>No. 1.</margin>

## Funeral honors rendered to the grandees of Peru after their death.

*The description of this is combined with the description of No. 2.*

---

<margin>No. 2.</margin>

## Manner of burying a grandee in *Peru*.

When an *Inca* <note>The term "Inca" here refers specifically to the ruler or members of the high nobility of the Incan Empire.</note>, or another grandee <note>original Dutch: "groote," referring to a person of high rank or a nobleman.</note> of the empire died, so many persons among his servants, friends, and even wives offered themselves—wishing to accompany him into the other world to serve him—that they could not all be buried with him, so that some of them were sent back. The body was carried, seated on a kind of throne, to the burial place; the wives and the servants followed the corpse, laden with provisions and food for the next life. During this procession, one of the closest relatives of the deceased blew some food into his mouth through a reed, so that he might be better able to make the journey. The image of the deceased, carved in wood, was placed upon his grave. A deceased artist was buried with the tools belonging to his profession and with the masterpieces of his art, and a warrior with his weapons. The two illustrations on this last plate show these ceremonies, including the manner of lowering the corpses into their graves.

<term>Peru</term> — <term>Incas</term> — <term>burial</term> — <term>honors</term> — <term>grave site</term> — <term>corpse</term> — <term>burial ritual</term>

<summary>This page describes the elaborate funeral customs of the Incan nobility, including voluntary human sacrifice by servants and wives, the provision of food for the afterlife, and the burial of professionals with their tools.</summary>

# PLATE CIV. NO. 1.

->FUNERAL HONORS, rendered to the NOBLES of Peru after their death.<-

---

<meta>No. 2.</meta>

->Manner of BURYING the NOBLES of Peru.<-

When an Inca <note>The term "Inca" here refers specifically to the sovereign ruler or high-ranking members of the imperial family of the Incan Empire.</note>, or another noble <note>original French: "Grands," referring to the "grandees" or high-ranking aristocracy of the region.</note> of the empire died, so many people—including his servants, friends, and even his wives—offered themselves to accompany him into the next world to serve him that they could not all be buried with him; as a result, many were sent away. 

The body was carried to the burial site while seated upon a type of throne. The wives and servants followed the corpse, carrying heavy loads of provisions and food intended for his use in the afterlife. During this procession, one of the closest relatives of the deceased would use a reed to blow food into the mouth of the deceased, believing this would better sustain him for the long journey ahead. An image of the deceased, carved from wood, was placed upon the grave as a marker. Furthermore, a deceased artist was buried alongside the tools of his trade and his most significant masterpieces, while a warrior was interred with his weapons. The two illustrations on this plate depict these solemn ceremonies and the specific methods used to lower the bodies into their final resting places.

To further recommend himself to the public, the publisher of the work of the late Mr. **Picart**—without increasing the price of 20 guilders <note>The "gulden" or guilder was the standard currency of the Netherlands at the time.</note> for which it was originally offered—wishes to add a very accurate and useful appendix under the title of: *Sacred ceremonies, religious exercises, and customs of the Reformed Church of the city and Canton of Zurich in Switzerland, presented in very fine plates and accompanied by a brief description, in three sections, in folio, by* **David Herrliberguer**, *1750.* 

This appendix is designed in such a way that it can not only be added to the original work of Mr. **Picart** as a continuation, but it can also serve as a separate work that is both accurate and educational. It is available separately with a brief French explanation for the price of 2 guilders, and with the High German <note>original: "Hoogduitschen," referring to the German language as used in the southern and central regions, including Switzerland.</note> text for 2 guilders and 45 kreuzer <note>The kreuzer (xr) was a smaller unit of currency; 60 kreuzer typically made up one guilder.</note>. The complete work of Mr. **Picart**, including the large High German text, is available at all times for the price of 36 guilders, calculated in High German currency.
